transfer-plan.md.text:
# Binding diversity and wording transfer study

Authorized continuation: target transfer after the small-set acquisition/retention result. Keep the fixed hierarchical architecture and split-rate policy, not trained plasticity endpoints. Each trial independently initializes from the same frozen scratch-English hierarchical best checkpoint with fresh optimizer. Use seed42, batch4/unroll128,2,000 QA +2,000 English rehearsal updates, fixed initial/final scores and no development-based checkpoint selection.

New original synthetic data seed904217:16 training labels,16 disjoint new development labels and16 disjoint new test labels. For familiar-name evaluation, reserve two disjoint balanced matchings of8 training-name pairs for development/test. A third disjoint matching of8 pairs covers all16 training names and forms the fixed control. Enlarge training to32 pairs (16 within-role,16 cross-role), including that fixed matching; offline role labels never enter prompts. Each larger-pool pair appears with2 complementary color pairs and both fact orders:128 complete four-question groups. Fixed control uses one color pair and both orders per fixed pair:16 groups. Assignment/query swaps are complete in every group. All train names are present in every arm; diverse-pool degrees vary and are reported.

Arms: fixed16 canonical grammar; diverse128 canonical grammar; mixed128 with the exact same facts, queries, candidates, labels and group IDs as diverse, but rendered using2 fact templates ×2 question templates. Assign one of4 combinations to each pair/color case, balanced across the64 cases, with both fact orders using the same combination. The fixed data is a fact-level subset of diverse data. Within each pair the larger pool covers all4 colors. Train facts keep both orderings, independent query entities and swapped assignments. Generator alone uses labels; neural scoring/training imports no symbolic inference logic.

Evaluation: six buckets = familiar-pair/new-name × base/alternate/heldout wording. Alternate uses the second training renderer; heldout uses a third fact and third question form absent from every training arm. Each bucket has8 pairs ×6 color combinations ×8 assignment/query/order conditions =384 questions/48 cases. Development and test have2,304 questions/288 cases each. Pair identities, names where required and exact text are split-disjoint. Names may occur in English pretraining; these are task-level splits. Each input fits128 bytes; no delay probe is added.

Every arm uses all its groups in shuffled cycles via the unchanged plasticity_run driver. Both128-group arms have identical underlying episodes and sampled group traces; only wording changes. Fixed versus diverse is update/supervised-byte/English-exposure matched, not repetitions-per-example matched:125 versus15–16 presentations per group. Input bytes differ with wording and are reported, while padded unroll/batch and answer supervision remain shared. This tests diversity at a fixed budget, not capacity or compute superiority. One seed/shared grammar/limited exposure restrict conclusions.

Test first: deterministic generation, full group and eight-condition validity, all-label coverage, within/cross balance, pair/name/text separation, reserved wording absence in training, paired canonical/mixed episode identity, fixed subset,128-byte bound, fresh-output guard and file hashes. Reuse the tested driver; add no model/optimizer changes. Review generator and split audit before freezing data/code/config/old source. Run required regression/static checks.

Train three fresh arms, retain source/config/protocol/environment/initial/final scores/counters/traces. Lock all3 endpoint hashes before opening test questions. Score six test buckets via neural likelihood and complete8 conditions, plus raw fixed examples per bucket, without extraction/repair. English development retention is reported; the repeatedly used English story test is not a new confirmation and will not be reopened. Predeclare acquisition/retention diagnostic complete training-group fraction≥0.875 and English-dev loss≤1.25×source. Reliable transfer is a separate gate: require≥0.9 complete cases in every fresh test bucket; report all failures, no sweeps or checkpoint promotion.

Deliver results/transfer/report.md, summary.json, checkpoint lock, dataset/trace/source audits and source/test/config/lock snapshots. Update research.md, prd.md, README.md and data/README.md. Preserve this frozen plan and previous sources/results. No Transformer-replacement, growing-category, arbitrary-device or chatbot-readiness claim follows from this study.

stream-plan.md.text:
# English and conversation training milestone

Approved intent: use public Hugging Face data to train and test MLM on English and dialogue.

- Download bounded source rows with provenance, response/content hashes, and source licensing links. Save JSONL so paragraphs and multi-turn conversations remain intact.
- Deterministic lanes consume all document bytes, carry recurrent state between chunks, freeze padded state, reset at new documents, and support exact sampler/carry recovery.
- Keep the original prefix command compatible. Add stream-train with fresh, resume, and parameter-only initialization modes. Chat adaptation uses explicit role labels and fresh optimizer state.
- Frozen full-document evaluation uses development data for selection and a separate test split only for reporting.
- Train a modest CPU configuration, save real loss curves and unedited generations, and document undertraining rather than infer understanding from loss.
- Add graph-free and plain recurrent comparison support where feasible; do not imply Transformer superiority without a matched comparison.


Execution: complete-document streaming, dataset download/preparation, English training, dialogue/rehearsal adaptation, qualitative probes, and before/after domain evaluation are complete. Twenty-one tests pass; review findings about generation message mode and interrupted best selection were reproduced and fixed. Source/metric artifacts are saved under results/english-chat. Plain-GRU/Transformer and independently trained graph-ablation baselines remain subsequent experiments; no topology advantage is claimed.

memory-plan.md.text:
# Retention-gate warm-start experiment

Goal: test whether longer initial recurrent retention improves context-sensitive reading without adding state or parameters. Authorized as the next memory experiment. No runtime solver or topology change.

Design: copy each architecture's English checkpoint into a fresh optimizer state. Add log(tau-1) only to its learned retention-gate bias, with tau geometrically spaced from 2 to 128 bytes. Graph distributes tau across nodes, GRU across hidden channels. Since h'=z*h+(1-z)*candidate and z=sigmoid(log(tau-1))=1-1/tau at zero other input, this sets a nominal retention prior, not a guaranteed actual timescale. Existing trained gate contributions remain, so this is chrono-inspired bias intervention, not the original chrono initialization algorithm.

Source: Tallec and Ollivier, https://arxiv.org/abs/1804.11188 . Saturation/slow writing may harm learning; failure remains reportable.

1. Add offline `mlm.memory_init` with finite range validation, source hash/provenance, fresh optimizer, output protection, no mutation of source. Tests verify only retention slice changes for both architectures, source preservation, unchanged budget, and checkpoint roundtrip.
2. Prepare two initial checkpoints from the same English sources used by assistant-learning. Freeze protocol before training. Reuse assistant-v2 data, seed/configuration, 2,000 updates and validation every 500; no hyperparameter sweep. No test data enters training/selection. Original unmodified assistant runs remain controls.
3. Run both stages, score development-selected checkpoints using frozen reading evaluation, then measure story retention. Existing tests are reused diagnostic sets: results are exploratory and need fresh confirmation before a positive generalization claim.
4. Save raw artifacts and report including negative outcomes. Update research, PRD and usage. Verify tests, lint and types. No git commit: workspace has no repository.


Execution complete: both models trained, development-selected checkpoints evaluated, raw artifacts and hash/exposure checks saved. The graph retains context longer and changes answers, but individual accuracy remains near chance and English retention worsens. No checkpoint promotion. Full regression: 36 tests pass; focused initializer tests and static checks pass after final output-protection change. See results/memory-retention/report.md.

README.md.text:
# Mini Learning Model

An experimental byte-level language model made of small GRU networks connected by a directed graph. JAX performs causal recurrent computation, Flax owns model parameters, and Optax trains them with clipped AdamW.

**Current state:** a tested fixed-graph CPU prototype with English training, matched GRU baselines, and controlled retrieval experiments. An optional learned node readout is implemented but has not solved entity binding. Dynamic growth, rewiring, continual parameter learning, and Transformer comparisons remain future experiments. This is not a general chatbot.

Read [the original idea and research](research.md), [requirements](prd.md), and [measured smoke results](results/smoke/report.md), [English/chat results](results/english-chat/report.md), and [baseline/reading comparison](results/comparison/report.md).

## Setup and checks

The tested environment is Linux x86-64 with Python 3.12 on CPU. uv selects the project Python; the system Python is not modified. GPU support has not been tested.

```sh
uv sync --locked
uv run pytest -q
uv run ruff check .
uv run ruff format --check .
uv run ty check src
```

## Train

```sh
uv run mlm train --train data/smoke/train.txt --validation data/smoke/validation.txt --config configs/smoke.json --out runs/my-first-mlm --steps 300 --eval-every 50
```

`--steps` means additional optimizer updates. Training uses independent document-prefix batches, with a fresh recurrent state per row. Documents are separated by blank lines. Documents longer than `length` are prefix-truncated; the summary reports truncation. This first trainer does not yet stream through all chunks of long documents. Choose appropriately short documents for now. Training/validation identical documents and identical scored prefixes are rejected, but this is not a full corpus decontamination system.

The included data is an original, deliberately simple fixture. It is not TinyStories. Validation is a development set used for checkpoint selection; use a separately prepared untouched test corpus for later research conclusions.

Outputs include:

- `best.mlm`: the best checkpoint among initial and periodic development evaluations.
- `latest.mlm`: latest resumable state, including optimizer state and sampling RNG.
- `metrics.jsonl`: periodically measured training/development metrics.
- `summary.json`: initial/final losses, best checkpoint, timing, memory, and truncation counts.
- `samples.json`: best-checkpoint prompts and greedy continuations.
- `config.json` and `environment.json`: settings, dependencies, backend, and source fingerprint.

Checkpoints use atomic single-file replacement, and state is committed before its metrics. Resume repairs a truncated final metric record while rejecting earlier corruption. Their stored topology is verified when loading. Runs are ignored by version control; small run evidence is preserved under results/.

## Generate and evaluate

```sh
uv run mlm generate runs/my-first-mlm/best.mlm --prompt 'The red ' --max-bytes 64
uv run mlm evaluate runs/my-first-mlm/best.mlm --data data/smoke/validation.txt
uv run mlm evaluate runs/my-first-mlm/best.mlm --data data/smoke/validation.txt --no-messages
```

Generation is greedy, stops at EOS, and changes recurrent state rather than weights. Display replaces invalid UTF-8 sequences. Disabling messages at evaluation tests dependence on graph communication; it is not a fair comparison against a separately trained graph-free baseline.

Loss and perplexity include structural targets where present. Bits/byte counts only payload bytes. Compare perplexities only with the same vocabulary and masking policy.

## Resume

```sh
uv run mlm train --train data/smoke/train.txt --validation data/smoke/validation.txt --out runs/my-first-mlm --resume runs/my-first-mlm/latest.mlm --steps 100
```

Resume restores configuration, parameters, Adam state, step count, and sampler RNG. Corpus identities must match. A nonempty output directory accepts only its own latest checkpoint and rejects newer history. To branch from a different or older checkpoint, use a new empty output directory. Best-checkpoint selection in a new branch starts with that branch's initial state.

## Implementation map

- `config.py`, `data.py`, `graph.py`: validation, byte batches, topology.
- `model.py`: independent GRUs and synchronous graph rounds inside a causal scan.
- `training.py`, `evaluate.py`: optimizer, masked loss, frozen-state evaluation.
- `checkpoint.py`, `generate.py`, `cli.py`: persistence and commands.
- `tests/`: causality, state isolation, NumPy reference, learnability, checkpoint/resume, split overlap, and output protection.

Next research milestone: isolate routing from memory timescales and pretraining mismatch, with retrieval and English retention measured separately. Multi-seed comparisons and a Transformer baseline remain outstanding.


## Train on real English and conversations

Prepare the bounded public datasets using [the data instructions](data/README.md). Then run:

```sh
uv run mlm stream-train --train data/hf/stories/train.jsonl --validation data/hf/stories/validation.jsonl --test data/hf/stories/test.jsonl --config configs/english.json --out runs/english-new --steps 4000 --eval-every 500
uv run mlm stream-train --train data/hf/mixed/train.jsonl --validation data/hf/mixed/validation.jsonl --test data/hf/mixed/test.jsonl --config configs/conversation.json --init runs/english-new/best.mlm --out runs/conversation-new --steps 2000 --eval-every 500
uv run mlm chat runs/conversation-new/best.mlm --message 'Hi!'
```

`stream-train` traverses entire documents. State carries between chunks and is detached for truncated backpropagation; padding freezes state and new documents reset it. Its checkpoints include recurrent carry, document order, per-lane positions, RNG, optimizer, and model state. `--resume` continues the same dataset/configuration; `--init` transfers parameters into a new stage with fresh optimizer and stream state. They are mutually exclusive. Changing datasets belongs to `--init`, not resume.

The conversation stage rehearses English stories. It learns all byte targets, including user turns, rather than assistant-only loss. `chat` is an experimental single-turn role wrapper, not evidence of instruction following or understanding. Inspect raw samples and held-out metrics before judging quality. `--no-messages` trains a graph-message ablation; the plain-GRU and message-ablation comparison is now recorded under results/comparison; a Transformer benchmark remains outstanding.

Evaluate whole documents explicitly:

```sh
uv run mlm evaluate runs/english-new/best.mlm --data data/hf/stories/test.jsonl --full-documents
```

The original `train` command retains its independent-prefix behavior for smoke reproduction. `evaluate` defaults to that historical prefix mode; use `--full-documents` for real-corpus runs. Development-selected test results are not used to update parameters or choose checkpoints. Repeated manual tuning on test results would invalidate that separation.


Current saved dialogue checkpoint: `runs/conversation-v1/best.mlm`. It learned a greeting but failed simple question probes. See the unedited results report; do not treat it as a capable assistant.


## Baselines and paired reading evaluation

Architecture selection is explicit in configuration: `architecture: "graph"` (default, including old checkpoints) or `architecture: "gru"`. The GRU is one recurrent cell with its own embedding/readout and no graph/message weights. For the GRU, `width` sets hidden size; graph-only `nodes`, `degree`, and `rounds` are ignored. `configs/gru-english.json` uses width 208, giving 368,210 parameters against the graph model's 366,722. A separate `--no-messages` graph ablation keeps the graph parameter arrays but disables neighbor information during both training and generation.

```sh
uv run mlm stream-train --train data/hf/stories/train.jsonl --validation data/hf/stories/validation.jsonl --test data/hf/stories/test.jsonl --config configs/english.json --out runs/no-messages-new --steps 4000 --eval-every 500 --no-messages
uv run mlm stream-train --train data/hf/stories/train.jsonl --validation data/hf/stories/validation.jsonl --test data/hf/stories/test.jsonl --config configs/gru-english.json --out runs/gru-new --steps 4000 --eval-every 500
uv run python -m mlm.comprehension runs/english-v1/best.mlm --out results/my-reading.json
```

The [paired reading suite](data/evaluation/README.md) is evaluation-only. Candidate answers are ranked using the frozen neural model's conditional byte likelihood; the answer key only grades results. It is not a keyword or regex answer generator. The paired contexts expose fixed-answer preferences that can score 50% on individual two-choice questions while getting every complete pair wrong. Chat-format diagnostic results should be reported separately from identically formatted English baselines.

Graph ablation retains at least 102,400 matrix parameters disconnected from data loss (the message projection and message-input half of GRU input matrices). Equal allocated parameter count therefore does not imply equal effective capacity. The plain-GRU comparison matches parameters approximately but has 208 recurrent-state scalars per sequence, versus 512 in the graph. Compare these as explicit architecture/resource trade-offs. One seed and these tiny subsets cannot establish general superiority.


The first matched English comparison is complete: story test losses were 1.122 for MLM, 1.157 without messages, and 1.099 for the parameter-matched plain GRU (lower is better). All tested checkpoints got zero fully correct pairs on the small reading diagnostic. These one-seed findings support further experiments rather than a superiority or comprehension claim. See [the full report](results/comparison/report.md).


## Assistant-only learning experiment

Assistant-only supervision and matched graph/GRU training are implemented. Both models completed 2,000 additional optimizer updates. Neither solved any of the 64 held-out counterfactual reading pairs; English story prediction also worsened. These checkpoints are experiments, not validated upgrades. See [results and reproduction commands](results/assistant-learning/report.md).

Prepare the offline supervised dataset from the existing public-data cache, then evaluate a saved checkpoint:

```sh
uv run python -m mlm.supervised_data --source data/hf --out data/assistant-v2
uv run python -m mlm.supervised_eval runs/assistant-graph-v1/best.mlm --out results/my-assistant-evaluation.json
```

Reuse existing prepared data instead of overwriting it. JSONL `loss_spans` are half-open UTF-8 byte offsets; `score_eos` controls EOS supervision. Input validity and supervision are separate: prompt bytes update recurrent state without contributing target loss. Full-text story rehearsal remains explicit. Use `stream-train` and `evaluate --full-documents` for supervised files; prefix commands reject them. Prompt-only batches advance memory without changing optimizer state or update count.

Streaming checkpoint selection follows global update multiples of `--eval-every`; off-grid endpoints save latest state but cannot replace best. Resume preserves supervision identity and the selection interval. Resuming into a fresh directory also restores the source best checkpoint; retain it alongside latest.

Synthetic labels are generated offline. Inference uses learned neural weights and recurrent state, with no label generator, regex answer solver, or response lookup. Names/templates are disjoint across the supervised reading splits; this does not guarantee those names were absent from English pretraining. Node growth, rewiring, and learned routing remain unimplemented.


## Retention experiment

An offline gate-bias intervention and reproducible memory probe are available. The graph now changes preferences with context, but individual reading accuracy remains around chance and English loss worsens. This is an experimental initialization change, not a validated architecture upgrade. See [protocol, results, and commands](results/memory-retention/report.md). Earlier English checkpoints remain the preferred references.


## Controlled retrieval curriculum

The latest experiment separates single-fact recall from selecting the queried person's fact. After 500 basic and 1,500 mixed binding/rehearsal updates, both graph and GRU answer all 96 single-fact test questions correctly across 0/64/128 filler bytes by candidate likelihood. Neither solves any of 96 complete multi-entity binding groups; multiple-fact accuracy remains around chance. These are narrow synthetic-task findings, not broad language understanding.

The [report](results/retrieval-curriculum/report.md) includes fresh-test checkpoint locks, all difficulty cells, raw greedy outputs, supervision exposure, and reproduction commands. English loss remains worse than the original English checkpoints, which are preserved.

```sh
uv run python -m mlm.retrieval_data --out data/retrieval-new --source data/hf
uv run python -m mlm.retrieval_eval runs/retrieval-binding-graph-v1/best.mlm --questions data/retrieval-v1/test-questions.json --out results/my-retrieval-evaluation.json
```

`retrieval_data` is offline dataset generation. `retrieval_eval` uses frozen neural answer likelihoods and evaluates context swaps plus fixed-context query swaps. Neither provides an inference-time answer solver. Tests after repeated tuning require fresh confirmation data.


## Focused binding and optional node readout

The latest [focused experiment](results/focused-binding/report.md) trains complete four-question groups with two people and no filler. Checkpoints are selected by complete development-group accuracy, with target loss as a tiebreaker. Graph, GRU, and a learned-readout graph each trained for 2,000 updates. Fresh-test complete groups: 0/56, 1/56, and 0/56. English prediction regressed, so these are not adopted upgrades.

The optional graph setting `node_readout: "attention"` adds 8,256 parameters and computes state-conditioned weights over current node states. Default `"sum"` preserves existing behavior and legacy checkpoints. This is learned neural pooling, not an explicit question parser, growing graph, or online parameter updates. Ordinary stream warm starts require the same readout setting; the experimental grouped runner can initialize new readout parameters while copying shared source tensors.

```sh
uv run python -m mlm.binding_data --out data/binding-new
uv run python -m mlm.binding_run --data data/binding-new --config configs/binding-graph.json --init runs/retrieval-basic-graph-v1/best.mlm --out runs/focused-binding-new --steps 2000 --eval-every 250
```

This dedicated runner starts a fresh optimizer and does not support resume. Use empty output paths. Every batch contains all four context/query swaps, with input validity separate from assistant loss masks. No story rehearsal is included in this diagnostic.

A separate post-hoc single-group sanity run achieves 4/4 correct rankings and raw greedy answers on its memorized training group. That demonstrates tiny-case learnability, not generalization. Next investigate gradual curriculum and optimization before expanding architecture. All 44 tests pass.


## Gradual binding comparison

The unchanged graph completed a 3,000-update curriculum and a matched flat-training control, both starting from the same memorized seed group. Curriculum fits 2/4/8/16 training groups completely, then 29/32 and 50/64. Both checkpoints were selected on development data and locked before testing.

Requiring every assignment/query swap and both sentence orders (eight questions per case), curriculum solves 18/24 familiar-name new-pair cases and 1/24 new-name cases. Flat solves 11/24 and 9/24. The source solves zero in either bucket. This is partial controlled-task transfer, not reliable chat or name-independent retrieval. A discovered early-role imbalance between familiar-name development and test pairs limits interpretation; see [the full report](results/gradual-binding/report.md). English prediction worsens severely, so no English/chat checkpoint is replaced.

```sh
uv run python -m mlm.gradual_data --out data/gradual-new
uv run python -m mlm.gradual_run --data data/gradual-new --config configs/gradual-graph.json --init runs/binding-overfit-sanity-v1/final.mlm --out runs/gradual-curriculum-new --strategy curriculum --stage-steps 500 --stories data/hf/stories/test.jsonl
uv run python -m mlm.gradual_eval runs/gradual-curriculum-new/best.mlm --questions data/gradual-new/test-questions.json --out results/gradual-curriculum-new.json
```

Use `--strategy flat` and a fresh output directory for the control. Finish and lock both development-selected models before testing. The standalone runner preserves optimizer state across its stages but does not implement resume. All 47 regression tests pass. Next: balanced confirmation splits, wider name diversity and an explicit English-retention strategy.


## Balanced confirmation and English rehearsal

The fresh [balanced study](results/balanced-confirmation/report.md) uses 32 training labels and balanced within/cross-role pairings. Both arms receive the same 2,000 QA updates from the preserved English checkpoint; rehearsal adds 2,000 English updates. All selected models score zero complete eight-condition cases on 96 familiar-name and 48 new-name test cases. This joint acquisition setting does not demonstrate binding. Source, learning rate and task size differ from the earlier toy-transfer experiment, so it is not a balancing-only replication.

Rehearsal preserves and slightly improves English test loss (1.121557 source to 1.087839). The unconstrained task-only candidate worsens it to 3.381755; its English-protected selection correctly falls back to source weights. Rehearsal's protected/unconstrained slots are the same trained model. Retention is a measured success; semantic binding is not. No general-chat model is promoted.

```sh
uv run python -m mlm.confirmation_data --out data/confirmation-new
uv run python -m mlm.confirmation_run --data data/confirmation-new --config configs/confirmation-graph.json --init runs/english-v1/best.mlm --out runs/confirmation-rehearsal-new --steps 2000 --eval-every 500 --rehearsal
```

`best-task.mlm` selects binding development accuracy without an English constraint. `best.mlm` additionally requires English development loss no more than 1.25 times the source baseline; step-zero fallbacks are explicitly recorded. This standalone runner has no resume feature. QA/English updates and bytes are counted separately; rehearsal costs extra compute. All 50 tests pass. Next diagnose source-controlled learning progression before more architecture changes.


## Hierarchical recurrent update prototype

A two-level learned router is implemented: four groups with two GRU nodes each. Config `node_update` selects `"dense"` (legacy default), `"uniform"` (fixed 1/N update rate), or `"hierarchical"` (learned group/child probabilities); `groups: 4` defines the hierarchy. The message graph and sum readout remain fixed. This is an unlabeled routing hierarchy, not trained verb/pronoun experts, a growing network, or a Transformer replacement.

The [three-arm pilot](results/hierarchical-routing/report.md) completes 1,000 QA + 1,000 English updates per model on fresh balanced data. All score 0/144 complete test cases. English test loss: dense 1.119035, uniform-slow 1.953038, hierarchical 1.473429. Learned routing improves on fixed slowing here, but does not beat the dense model or demonstrate binding. Initial slowing already changes the dense-trained source's behavior; this is a warm-start pilot, not matched pretraining from scratch.

```sh
uv run python -m mlm.confirmation_data --out data/hierarchy-new --seed 920231
uv run python -m mlm.hierarchy_run --data data/hierarchy-new --config configs/hierarchy-hierarchical.json --init runs/english-v1/best.mlm --out runs/hierarchy-new --steps 1000 --eval-every 250
```

Use the dedicated hierarchy runner for routing-balance auxiliary loss and usage diagnostics. Ordinary trainers support the forward model but do not add that auxiliary loss. `best.mlm` in this runner selects binding development score/QA loss without an English constraint. Standard stream warm starts require matching update modes; the experimental initializer copies shared source weights into variants. Soft routing computes every node, so no sparse speedup is claimed. All 54 tests pass. Source code, tests, config and lockfile snapshots are preserved with the report.


## From-scratch dense versus hierarchical study

The [new comparison](results/from-scratch/report.md) independently pretrains both architectures for 4,000 English updates, then adapts each own checkpoint on fresh balanced binding with English rehearsal. Shared initial tensors and data budgets are audited; selections are locked before tests. Separate sanity probes demonstrate small-set memorization, while the full report distinguishes it from held-out binding and English retention. CPU timing and tensor sizes are measured with explicit limits. All 56 tests pass. The model remains an experimental fixed recurrent graph; growing experts and Transformer replacement are unproven.


## Binding acquisition diagnostic

The [nested-set study](results/acquisition/report.md) tests independent 1/4/16/64-group task-only trials from each architecture's own English checkpoint. It reports training fit separately from held-out development transfer, actual subset name coverage and English forgetting. Paired source resets, subset IDs, sample traces and byte budgets are audited. These are exploratory fixed-endpoint trials, with no test-based selection or promoted chat model.


## Equal-exposure acquisition control

The [exposure study](results/exposure/report.md) gives each of 16 training groups 125 presentations in 2,000 task-only updates, matching the per-group exposure of the successful four-group trials. It preserves the architecture, source and learning rate; paired traces/bytes and source fingerprints are audited. Results distinguish training fit, eight-condition development transfer and English forgetting. This is a development-only diagnostic with no promoted model.


## Shared/node rates and rehearsal

Config supports optional shared_lr_scale, node_lr_scale and router_lr_scale (default 1). They scale completed AdamW updates, including decay; checkpoint loading restores the policy. The [six-arm study](results/plasticity/report.md) compares uniform high/low rates and slower shared representations, with and without English rehearsal. It reports binding acquisition, development transfer and English retention separately, and counts the extra rehearsal compute. Existing graph/default behavior is preserved; no chatbot is promoted.


## Pairing and wording transfer study

The [fresh transfer study](results/transfer/report.md) compares a fixed pool, varied pairings/colors, and the same episodes with varied wording. Three source-matched rehearsal trials are locked before scoring reserved test pairings, names and wording. Every arm covers all training labels; source, exposure differences, raw neural rankings/generations and complete eight-condition test outcomes are explicit. No architecture or default-checkpoint replacement is claimed.


## Learned associative memory pilot

Optional Config.memory="delta" adds a learned read-before-write key/value matrix to the graph; memory_keys controls its row count and memory_lr_scale its optimizer rate. Default memory="none" remains compatible with existing checkpoints. Matrix state is document-local, reset/frozen/carried with the recurrent state; it is not permanent learning during chat. The [paired pilot](results/associative/report.md) records source-preserving zero-gate initialization, fresh locked binding tests, English retention and the added parameter/state/runtime costs. All 68 regression tests pass.


## Memory addressing diagnostics

[Report](results/addressing/report.md): actual-forward tracing, exact signed overwrite-aware reads, projected region vectors and frozen readout ablation. Graph and delta memorize one training group; both fail the four-group fixed-budget probe. This is a training diagnostic, with unequal per-group exposure and no new test claims. New helpers live in `src/mlm/addressing.py`; the archived fixed-protocol recipe is `results/addressing/recipe.py` and expects fresh output directories. It refuses to overwrite prior probe runs. Projection postprocessing is `uv run python results/addressing/project_regions.py`.


## Four-group exposure control

[Report](results/addressing-exposure/report.md): at2,000QA+2,000English updates, delta fits all4 training groups while the graph control fits0/4. Disabling delta's frozen memory output removes that fitted success. Both still fail complete groups in the tiny reused development case. This is single-seed acquisition evidence, with extra memory parameters and additional total rehearsal compared with earlier probes. The frozen protocol contains exact reproduction commands; existing run directories must be preserved.


## Adaptation-seed replication

[Report](results/addressing-replication/report.md): the seed42 four-group delta fit did not repeat at predefined seeds43/44 (8/16 and9/16 training rankings;0/4 groups both). Graph controls score8/16 and0/4. All retain English performance but fail complete tiny development groups. This is fixed-source adaptation replication, not independent English pretraining. The new acquisition gate fails0/2; no model is promoted. Exact commands, frozen inputs, logs, checkpoints and endpoint audits are preserved.


## Initialization and training schedule control

[Report](results/addressing-factorial/report.md): in a selected2×2 table, both memory initializations42/43 acquire all4 training groups with combined schedule42; both fail all4 with schedule43. Two cells are new and two are reused historical runs. This is a conditional schedule lead, not generalization or a reversal of the failed replication gate. All203 input/artifact audits pass. associative-plan.md.text:
# Learned delta-memory architecture pilot

Authorized continuation after the transfer-data study. Add an opt-in causal learned key/value fast-state matrix to the fixed graph, then compare against the unchanged graph. This implements a published delta-rule principle (https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.11174; https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.06484), not a new algorithm or a reproduction of DeltaNet's full training/parallel kernels.

Config.memory = none|delta (default none), memory_keys=16 (4..128), memory_lr_scale=1 (finite,positive,≤1). Delta memory supports graph/sum readout only. Default/legacy config parsing, parameter shapes, state shapes and math remain unchanged. Register memory parameters as a separate optimizer role. Keep node/router rates0.003 and shared representations0.0003; memory rate0.003. Standard stream warm starts must match memory settings; dedicated experimental warm_start may add zero-gated parameters. Checkpoint load rebuilds the correct model/state/optimizer from config.

State is packed as [B,nodes+memory_keys,width] in delta mode: first nodes rows are graph-GRU state, remaining rows are a memory matrix M[K,D]. Default shape remains [B,nodes,width]. Per token: reset graph and matrix on document reset; run the same graph; features=concat(current embedding,tanh(base pooled graph output)); normalized learned key k and query q, tanh learned value v, sigmoid learned write gate beta. Read r=q^T M_old and update M_new=M_old+beta*k*(v-k^T M_old)^T. Add gain*(r@output_kernel) to base graph readout before existing normalization/head. gain initializes exactly0. Both states freeze on invalid padding, even if reset=True. Reads use no future token, and state carries across chunks. This is document-local inference state, not inference-time gradient learning or persistent external database retrieval.

Shapes at8 nodes/width64/keydim16: persistent state grows from512 to1,536 floats (2,048→6,144 bytes/sequence). Expected added parameters16,514 (base368,270→384,784). All learned projections/write/gain live in memory role; no categories/names/labels enter inference. Matrix state is transient, reset per document, and uses a dense sequential reference implementation. No growth, sparse execution or speed advantage claimed.

Tests first: delta overwrite/read with orthogonal keys, key interference, beta0, finite gradients; source-compatible zero-gate predictions and base initial tensors; causality/prefix chunk equivalence; reset and invalid-padding preservation for entire packed carry; route shape remains true graph nodes; open-gate gradients into every memory tensor; checkpoint/optimizer continuation and config/role guards. Test one genuine optimizer update through make_routed_step and stream carrying. Full regression/static checks and independent review before freezing training.

Experiment: baseline versus delta, fresh own English source from runs/scratch-english-hierarchical-v1/best.mlm, zero-gated warm start only; never load old QA endpoints. New transfer_data seed638101 produces fixed/diverse/mixed pools, but only the diverse128-group pool is trained here. Same split rates, seed42, batch4/unroll128,2,000 QA +2,000 English updates each, independent fresh optimizers, fixed initial/final evaluation. English initial loss/predictions must match, while extra parameters/state/compute are explicitly counted. This is source-preserving adaptation, not independently pretrained superiority or an exact parameter/state-matched architecture ablation. The unused fixed/mixed variants are data artifacts, not additional trained arms.

Training inputs and source/code/config/data hashes freeze before runs. Do not use previous transfer test data as fresh confirmation. Lock both final checkpoint hashes before scoring all six new test buckets, plus original English source baseline. Test reliable transfer requires≥90% complete8-condition cases in every bucket. Acquisition/retention diagnostic requires≥87.5% complete training groups and English-dev loss≤1.25×source. No model selection/promotion/sweeps, no reopening English test. Report candidate rankings and raw fixed examples without answer repair; inability to fit128 groups at15–16 repetitions is not a capacity proof. One seed/narrow grammar/source adaptation remain limits.

After training and evaluation finish, benchmark both endpoints sequentially in fresh CPU processes with runtime_bench (B1,lengths32/128/512,5 warmups,30 timings); report tensor/state bytes and inclusive process RSS. No Transformer, generation-latency or arbitrary-device claims. Archive source/tests/config/lock snapshots, results/associative/report.md +summary.json +locks/audits and update research.md/prd.md/README.md/data docs. Preserve this frozen plan and older models/results; execution status separate.

Numerical preflight finding: packed-state CPU scan compilation changes float32 fusion, with maximum logit delta5.96e-7 and graph-state delta3.73e-9 on the tiny zero-gate fixture. Eager execution is bitwise identical. Zero-gate functional equality is mathematical; compiled checks use1e-6 absolute/relative tolerance and initial full-English loss must agree within1e-5. Do not claim compiled bitwise identity between differing state layouts.

# Gradual binding curriculum

Approved: scale from the already memorized four-question group through more groups, measure novel pairings of familiar names separately from new-name transfer, leave architecture unchanged and monitor English.

Use the sum-readout graph, source runs/binding-overfit-sanity-v1/final.mlm, fresh optimizer at LR 0.003 (the successful sanity LR), batch four, unroll 128, seed 42. The source already has 500 updates of single-group memorization; report that separately. Preserve all sources.

Data: training-name pool Dan/Ned/Ada/Ben/Cal/Eli/Fay/Gus. Reserve four unordered pairs for known-name development and four different pairs for known-name test, each covering all eight names. Remaining 20 pairs supply a deterministic nested 64-group training pool. First group exactly reproduces the source's Dan/Ned gold/blue sanity example; first four groups introduce all eight names, next four reverse their fact order. Add color diversity, then additional name pairings. All four assignment/query swaps remain in each batch. No rehearsal or architecture change. New-name development and test use separate eight-name pools and four disjoint entity pairs per pool. Every evaluation pair includes all six color pairs and both fact orders: 48 complete groups / 192 questions per bucket. Exact texts and held-out pair identities cannot overlap training.

Two arms, identical source and total budget. Curriculum: 500 updates each at 2,4,8,16,32,64 groups, carrying the same optimizer continuously. Flat: 3,000 updates over all 64 groups from the start. Reset recurrent state for independent examples, shuffle complete groups. Evaluate initial state and every 500 updates. Record actual names seen; early familiar-name-pool scores must disclose names not yet trained for binding.

Select among stage endpoints at updates 1,000–3,000 after all eight training names have actually been seen, maximizing macro-average development complete-group accuracy across the two fixed equal-sized buckets, then minimizing combined target loss; exact ties keep earlier state. Training scores and English retention do not select checkpoints. Save latest and selected best, stage groups/steps, source/data hashes and RNG/order/cursor. Tests: nested group counts and first group source-text match, diverse partner coverage, zero exact-text overlap, known-pair partition disjointness, new-name partitioning, balanced four-question groups/masks and unroll limits. # Focused two-person binding experiment

Approved next step: isolate one distractor, zero filler, varied name pairings and fact order, with complete context/query groups as the primary development metric. Keep graph and GRU controls. No inference solver.

Data: all unordered pairs of 16 training names, plus separate eight-name development and test pools. Each pair gets one of six unordered color pairs, cycling in shuffled entity-pair order, with both fact orders. Each order has four questions: two swapped color assignments crossed with two queried people. Each update consumes one complete group of four examples, using assistant-only byte loss and EOS. No story rehearsal in this diagnostic; measure English retention separately. This removes the previous unaccounted supervision imbalance. Grammar and four known four-byte colors are shared intentionally. Names are disjoint within this task, not globally novel.

Train from the corresponding basic-stage single-fact checkpoints, not previous binding/test-selected weights. Fresh optimizer, seed 42, batch four, unroll 128, learning rate 0.0005, 2,000 updates; evaluate at zero and every 250. Select by highest complete binding-group accuracy, then lowest assistant-target development loss; exact ties keep the earlier checkpoint. Every example fits one unroll. Shuffle groups, not individual documents. Save byte counters and sampler identity. No resume support claimed by this dedicated runner; refuse nonempty output directories.

If both controls have not demonstrated the intended binding and graph development group accuracy is below 90%, run one predetermined graph readout variant at the same budget before opening test data. Variant: additive learned node attention conditioned on node zero's recurrent state (the initially fastest-retention node), with keys from all current nodes. It is state-conditioned, not an explicit parsed question encoder. Initialize attention scores to zero so uniform weighting reproduces the old pooled readout when shared weights are copied. Scaling sqrt(nodes) preserves the old sum/sqrt(nodes) convention. Extra parameters must be reported; this is not a parameter-matched architecture comparison. It neither adds per-token Transformer attention nor growing topology. Decision depends only on development, not test.

Implement offline binding_data.py, grouped binding_run.py, and regression tests first. Test complete/varied group construction, labels and masks, shuffled full-group batches, input limits, selection priority, source integrity and output protection. # Assistant-only learning and held-out reading milestone

Approved intent: improve MLM's learning objective and reading ability, compare with the parameter-matched GRU before structural growth.

- Keep input validity separate from target supervision. Structured assistant byte spans define loss targets. Prompt bytes still update memory. EOS supervision is explicit. No regex/keyword response solver is added.

- Build supervised reading data with deterministic labels, balanced counterfactual pairs, disjoint entity names and wording templates across train/development/test. Keep reading-v1 unchanged and out of training. Label-generation rules live only in offline dataset preparation.

research.md.text:
# Mini Learning Model (MLM): Research and Feasibility

Date: 2026-10-23
Status: Initial research synthesis and proposed experimental direction.
Evidence: Public papers and official project documentation consulted during the project discussion. No architecture has been implemented or benchmarked in this workspace.
Companion document: [Product requirements](prd.md).

## 1. Preserve the original idea

The founder's idea is a new language-model architecture named **Mini Learning Model**: small neural networks connected by nodes and edges like a spiderweb. A dot can itself contain a smaller web of computational units. Nodes and connections can grow, change, and reorganize rather than remaining a permanently fixed structure. The model should eventually adapt during use and aim for smaller size, lower computation, faster execution, and broad device accessibility.

The ambition is to investigate an alternative to Transformers, not merely rename a small Transformer. The spiderweb metaphor is the starting intuition; it is not yet a mathematical architecture or evidence of better performance.

Preserve these essential ideas:

- Small neural modules as the computational building blocks.
- Sparse communication between modules.
- Potential hierarchy: modules may contain internal subnetworks.
- Learned selection of useful computation.
- Adaptive connectivity and bounded capacity growth.
- Investigation of learning or memory updates during operation.
- Practical efficiency measured on actual hardware.

The initial prototype will simplify this vision deliberately. A fixed graph comes first; growth, hierarchy, and continual adaptation remain explicit later research stages rather than forgotten requirements.

Terminology: MLM here means Mini Learning Model, not the established abbreviation for masked language modeling. The initial objective is causal next-token prediction.

## 2. Assessment

A research prototype is technically feasible. Existing work supports individual mechanisms such as sparse rewiring, capacity expansion, recurrence, and neural memory updates during inference. The reviewed evidence does not establish that their combination will outperform Transformers or run at useful quality and speed on every device.

Confidence assessment:

| Claim | Assessment |
|---|---|
| Small neural modules can communicate through a graph | Established computational approach; our specific implementation is untested |
| Connectivity can change during training | Supported by dynamic sparse training research |
| Capacity can expand across tasks | Supported in continual-learning settings |
| A language model can update neural memory during inference | Supported by TTT and Titans research |
| Our proposed graph will improve language quality per unit of compute | Open hypothesis |
| Arbitrary sparsity will produce lower latency | Not established; depends on kernels and hardware |
| The exact proposed combination is novel | Undetermined; requires a more systematic novelty review |
| One implementation can deliver useful operation on every device | Not a credible initial requirement |

## 3. Separate the forms of adaptation

1. **State adaptation:** recurrent activations change with each token; model parameters need not change.
2. **Routing adaptation:** different tokens activate different modules or edges.
3. **Topology adaptation:** connections are added, removed, or redirected.
4. **Parameter adaptation:** trainable weights change through learning.
5. **Capacity adaptation:** additional trainable modules or parameters are allocated.
6. **Memory adaptation:** a dedicated state or learned memory is updated during a sequence or session.

These must have separate switches and measurements. An animated graph or changing hidden state is not proof of structural growth. Ordinary LLMs update weights during training and generally keep them fixed during inference; they are not inherently incapable of adaptation.

## 4. Related research and projects

### 4.1 Dynamic sparse connectivity: RigL

[Rigging the Lottery: Making All Tickets Winners](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.11134), with [official code](https://github.com/google-research/rigl), learns connectivity by removing and adding connections during training using weight and gradient information.

Relevance: supports changing a sparse network's wiring rather than assuming fixed wiring is optimal. Its principal setup maintains a fixed parameter budget; it does not establish the benefits of unlimited growth or our graph-of-modules design. Gradient-based growth scoring also has a computational cost that must be counted.

### 4.2 Capacity growth: Dynamically Expandable Networks

[Lifelong Learning with Dynamically Expandable Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/1708.01547) selectively retrains and expands a network across tasks, including mechanisms intended to limit semantic drift.

Relevance: growth is a legitimate continual-learning mechanism. Limitation: task-sequence results cannot be assumed to transfer to open-ended language modeling or autonomous growth on arbitrary user text.

### 4.3 Local growth: neural cellular automata

[Growing Neural Cellular Automata](https://distill.pub/2020/growing-ca/) demonstrates learned local update rules that grow and regenerate patterns from seeds.

Relevance: a useful conceptual connection to local communication, shared rules, and self-organization. Limitation: growth of active cell states is different from creating new trainable capacity. Pattern regeneration is not evidence of language understanding.

### 4.4 Neural memory: Test-Time Training

[Learning to (Learn at Test Time): RNNs with Expressive Hidden States](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.04620), with [official PyTorch implementation](https://github.com/test-time-training/ttt-lm-pytorch), treats recurrent hidden state as a small learning model updated on test sequences.

Relevance: particularly close to small networks acting as adaptive memory. Limitation: neural memory introduces computation, state, and optimization complexity; its benefits must be demonstrated separately from topology growth.

### 4.5 Neural memory: Titans

[Titans: Learning to Memorize at Test Time](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.00663) investigates neural long-term memory that learns during inference.

Relevance: informs a later memory subsystem. Limitation: adaptive memory does not by itself imply a growing graph, permanent factual learning, or low inference cost.

### 4.6 Nonstandard sequence backbones: Mamba and RWKV

[Mamba](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.00752), with [official implementation](https://github.com/state-spaces/mamba), investigates selective state-space sequence modeling. [RWKV](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13048) investigates recurrent language modeling with parallelizable training formulations.

Relevance: language modeling need not rely on standard full self-attention. Their results are architecture- and setting-specific; reported speedups are not predictions for MLM. Recurrent formulations compress past context into state, creating capacity and retrieval trade-offs.

### 4.7 Small language experiments: TinyStories

[TinyStories](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.07759) demonstrates coherent story generation in a restricted distribution with models below 10 million parameters.

Relevance: an accessible first language-learning experiment. Limitation: coherent simple stories do not establish broad reasoning, factual knowledge, multilingual competence, or general assistant quality.

## 5. Candidate approaches

| Approach | Strength | Main risk | Position |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sparse recurrent graph of small modules | Direct test of the founder's concept | Routing, optimization, and irregular execution overhead | Recommended research direction |
| Established recurrent backbone plus adaptive memory | Stronger reference point and fewer simultaneous unknowns | Less architectural departure | Baseline or fallback |
| Cellular-automata language model | Strong local self-organization emphasis | Most speculative language-learning and execution behavior | Later exploratory branch |

A graph is not automatically attention-free. If every module scores every other module each token, routing may reintroduce expensive all-pairs computation. Candidate-neighbor sets and bounded degree should be the initial assumption.

## 6. Proposed architecture, not a validated design

### 6.1 Data flow

Token IDs → embeddings → input injection → recurrent graph updates → graph readout → vocabulary logits → next-token loss.

The graph persists within a sequence. Its state resets at independent sequence boundaries by default. Reading position t must never depend on token t+1 or later. Prediction and state-update ordering must be documented explicitly.

### 6.2 Modules and graph

Each module contains a small gated update network and a state vector. Nodes initially share a width so their execution can be batched. A bounded number of neighbor edges carries messages; an explicit readout produces token predictions. Begin with a flat graph. Nested subnetworks and multiple graph levels are later ablations.

An illustrative update is:

m_i = aggregate over selected neighbors j of gate(i,j,input) * message(h_j)

h_i_next = gated_update(h_i, m_i, input)

This is a conceptual family, not the final equation. Choose normalization, parameter sharing, update order, and readout through small controlled experiments. Synchronous updates must read previous-step states so execution order does not silently change the model.

### 6.3 Routing

First run all modules in the small fixed graph. Add input-dependent routing later. A hard top-k operation does not provide ordinary gradients through the discrete selection itself; a later design must specify a training method and compare its cost. Track module usage and collapse onto a few modules.

### 6.4 Growth and rewiring

Run the structural controller between training intervals, not in every token computation initially. Consider removing persistently unused edges, adding candidate connections, or activating modules after sustained evidence of a capacity bottleneck. Loss spikes alone are insufficient evidence: they may indicate bad data, optimization problems, or domain shift.

Every structural event needs a reason, resource-budget check, initialization rule, optimizer-state update, graph-invariant check, and checkpoint. Growth must be compared against a model with the same final capacity from the beginning.

### 6.5 Memory and online learning

Separate ordinary recurrent state from optional fast-weight memory and durable parameter updates. Default evaluation keeps learned model parameters frozen. Later test-time learning must specify which variables change, available supervision, learning rate, reset boundaries, retention tests, and rollback behavior. Never use hidden evaluation labels for adaptation.

The user accepted the stack discussion and requested project documents. The last recommended default was JAX + Flax; no versions or target hardware have been selected. Record this as the **working proposal**, not an explicit user choice between every framework.

| Training and numerical research | JAX + Flax | Differentiation, compiled tensor computation, neural modules |

### 7.1 JAX and growth

[JAX JIT documentation](https://docs.jax.dev/en/latest/201/jit.html) explains specialization and recompilation when shapes or static values change. Use fixed-shaped edge arrays, parameter pools, states, and active masks within a capacity stage. Updating edge-index values can express rewiring without changing array shapes. Increase physical capacity at explicit checkpoints, accepting recompilation and optimizer-state migration.

Logical activation of reserved slots is not physical allocation growth. Allocated parameters, trainable parameters, active parameters, serialized size, and executed work must be reported separately. A dense calculation followed by masking does not constitute sparse execution.

[Flax NNX documentation](https://flax.readthedocs.io/en/latest/guides/pytree.html) describes module and state integration. A Flax object graph is a software abstraction, not automatically the learned spiderweb topology.

### 7.2 Framework alternatives

- [Burn](https://github.com/tracel-ai/burn): strongest considered Rust-first alternative for training and inference; validate required operations on the intended backend.
- [Candle](https://github.com/huggingface/candle): supports training and custom operations, with useful Rust deployment examples; proposed primarily for a later runtime evaluation.
- [tinygrad](https://docs.tinygrad.org/): attractive for framework-level experimentation; adds the risk of dividing attention between model and framework engineering.
- PyTorch: remains a practical eager-execution fallback if structural experiments prove cumbersome in JAX.

Choose one primary training implementation. Porting a novel graph requires behavior and state semantics, not just loading its weights.

### 7.3 Mojo

Mojo is allowed and remains an option. [Its documentation](https://docs.modular.com/mojo/manual/) describes Python interoperability; [binding limitations](https://docs.modular.com/mojo/manual/python/mojo-from-python/) and [hardware requirements](https://docs.modular.com/mojo/requirements/) must be checked against the pinned release and target device.

A Mojo operation used for training needs correct gradients and integration with the host framework. Python importability is not sufficient for compilation, autodiff, or zero-copy device access. [JAX FFI](https://docs.jax.dev/en/latest/ffi.html) is a possible integration mechanism, not proof of a ready-made Mojo backend. Compare any kernel with a reference implementation and include call, synchronization, and transfer costs.

## 8. Experimental program

### Stage A: Establish a trustworthy evaluation pipeline

Select one target machine and record CPU, GPU, RAM, operating system, framework versions, dtype, and power settings where available. Establish deterministic data splits and a common tokenizer. Train a small Transformer and a gated recurrent baseline with equivalent preprocessing.

### Stage B: Fixed graph

Use an exploratory total parameter range of about 1–10 million, adjustable to hardware. Verify causal correctness, finite gradients, checkpoint resume, state reset, and ability to overfit a tiny training subset. Then evaluate held-out data. This range is a proposal, not a proven optimum.

### Stage C: Routing and rewiring

Introduce routing separately from rewiring. Compare each against the fixed graph and account for controller and scoring costs. Keep a random-rewiring control where feasible to distinguish learned selection from generic perturbation.

### Stage D: Bounded growth

Compare against fixed models with the same initial capacity, same final capacity, and approximately matched total training compute. Include a reserved-but-inactive pool control to distinguish new physical capacity from activating preallocated parameters.

### Stage E: Continual adaptation

Use a documented domain sequence. Evaluate new-domain learning and old-domain retention after each stage. Compare memory-only adaptation, parameter updates, growth-only, and their combinations. Distinguish session-specific adaptation from durable learning.

### Stage F: Runtime optimization

Only after correctness and a repeatable learning result, optimize the measured bottleneck. Evaluate CPU inference first on the selected device, then other devices individually. Custom Mojo or Rust kernels are justified by measured end-to-end benefit.

## 9. Measurements and comparison rules

Required: held-out negative log-likelihood, perplexity with a common tokenizer, peak host/device memory, checkpoint bytes, parameter counts, training wall time, first-token latency, steady generation throughput, and structural-controller overhead.

For a recurrent graph, report node count, edge count, degree, update rounds per token, selected modules, and executed operations where measurable. Track allocation growth, compile time, and recompilation count. Include adaptation memory and optimizer state in relevant measurements.

Benchmark timings must synchronize asynchronous device work and separate compilation/warm-up from steady execution. Use identical prompts, sequence lengths, batch sizes, and generation settings. Report at least three training seeds for headline research claims, with mean and dispersion; initial smoke runs may use one seed and must be labeled accordingly.

Matched parameter count and matched compute are different comparisons. Report both when claiming efficiency. A lower loss at higher cost is not an efficiency win. Energy claims require actual measurements or an explicitly identified estimate with methodology.

## 10. Main risks and mitigations

| Risk | Mitigation / experiment |
|---|---|
| Sparse work is slower than dense work | Benchmark actual gather, aggregation, and routing kernels |
| Local graph cannot retrieve distant context | Retrieval probes and controlled message-depth or shortcut experiments |
| Growth increases memory without quality gains | Hard budgets and fixed-final-capacity control |
| Routing collapses | Usage metrics and controlled routing alternatives |
| Continual learning forgets old domains | Retention evaluation, replay or selective updates as later ablations |
| Training leaks future tokens | Causality tests covering graph state and memory updates |
| Structural changes corrupt resume | Serialize topology, optimizer state, RNG state, and controller state |
| JAX compilation dominates | Fixed capacity stages, bounded shapes, compile-time reporting |
| Too many languages delay research | Single reference implementation before native kernels |
| Apparent novelty duplicates existing work | Focused related-work review once equations and controller are specified |

## 11. Research success and stopping rules

A working graph language model is an engineering milestone, not evidence of superiority. A research success requires a reproducible advantage on a declared quality/resource or adaptation/retention comparison. Exact improvement thresholds must be set after baseline variance and hardware costs are known, before the main comparison run.

If a feature repeatedly fails to improve the relevant comparison under a documented tuning budget, record the negative result and simplify or revise it. Do not add hierarchy, routing, growth, and test-time learning together to hide an unexplained failure.

## 12. Open decisions

- Available training hardware and resource budget.
- First inference device, RAM ceiling, and useful latency target.
- Confirmation of JAX + Flax versus a Rust-first Burn implementation.
- Dataset subset, tokenizer, sequence length, and training-token budget.
- Initial module equations, degree, state width, and readout.
- Definition and timing of the first structural-growth experiment.
- Whether eventual online learning is session-local or durable.

## 13. Evidence boundaries

This is a targeted initial literature and tooling review, not an exhaustive systematic survey or novelty certification. Paper demonstrations apply to their own experimental conditions. Framework capabilities and backend support can change; pin versions and recheck official documentation before implementation. All architecture choices above are proposals until tested.


## 14. Follow-up: the two mini-AGI repositories

Reviewed: 2026-10-23. Method: read repository documentation, configuration, and selected source files through public web access. Neither project was installed, executed, trained, or independently benchmarked. Links below target moving main branches, not pinned snapshots; cached GitHub and raw views showed different run counters. Reproduction must first pin a commit and matching weights/configuration. Do not combine counters from different snapshots.

### 14.1 muellerberndt/mini-agi: an agent layer

[Repository](https://github.com/muellerberndt/mini-agi); [inspected miniagi.py](https://github.com/muellerberndt/mini-agi/blob/main/miniagi.py).

The inspected implementation constructs external language-model clients for action selection and summarization. It builds prompts containing objectives, prior observations, and optional criticism, then interprets commands. Its memory is application context and summarized history. This is useful agent orchestration, but it does not implement MLM's growing trainable graph or demonstrate a new neural backbone.

Possible later use: a model-independent task loop for evaluating an already capable MLM. It should not be the initial architecture foundation. An agent's apparent improvement from summaries or tool feedback must not be counted as neural parameter learning.

### 14.2 volotat/mini-AGI: relevant model-level engineering

[Repository](https://github.com/volotat/mini-AGI); [README](https://github.com/volotat/mini-AGI/blob/main/README.md).

The author describes a toy continual-learning byte model trained on an 8 GB GPU, with a growing expert pool backed by disk. This is much closer to MLM's capacity-adaptation goal. The README also explicitly says generation does not train the weights. Shared forward code is not equivalent to learning on every generated token.

The reported continual-learning experiments favor a slower shared trunk and interleaving. They do not establish elimination of forgetting in arbitrary streams. Published examples are undertrained and include clear errors; project naming is not evidence of AGI. These are author-reported findings, not results reproduced here.

Source-level observations:

| Inspected source | Observation | Implication for MLM |
|---|---|---|
| [model.py](https://github.com/volotat/mini-AGI/blob/main/minagi/model.py) | PyTorch decoder components include attention, rotary positions, RMSNorm, and SwiGLU | This is not evidence of an attention-free replacement |
| [recur.py](https://github.com/volotat/mini-AGI/blob/main/minagi/recur.py) | Reuses blocks with learned halting and a PonderNet-style objective | Adaptive depth is different from adding modules |
| [paged.py](https://github.com/volotat/mini-AGI/blob/main/minagi/paged.py) | Implements disk/RAM/device expert residency, per-expert state handling, and stable identities | A useful engineering reference for later offloading |
| [pool.py](https://github.com/volotat/mini-AGI/blob/main/minagi/pool.py) | Contains expert routing, pool expansion, pruning, and distinct resident-pool behavior | Do not assume all pool variants follow one growth/pruning rule |
| [plasticity.py](https://github.com/volotat/mini-AGI/blob/main/minagi/plasticity.py) | Adjusts learning rate using held-out observations | Such data is a development/control set, not an untouched final test |
| [forgetting_probe.py](https://github.com/volotat/mini-AGI/blob/main/replication/forgetting_probe.py) | Provides before/after domain scoring, sequential/interleaved modes, and optimizer-state controls | Useful experiment structure; not independent validation |

The [inspected configuration](https://github.com/volotat/mini-AGI/blob/main/config.yaml) specifies a 512-wide trunk, eight attention heads, an initial 64 experts, top-8 selection, and 32 resident experts. These are reference-project settings, not MLM defaults. At those dimensions, a three-matrix SwiGLU expert has approximately 3 × 512 × 2048 = 3,145,728 matrix parameters. An initially modest active footprint can therefore coexist with hundreds of millions of stored expert parameters.

Inference: paging expands accessible capacity but does not make total storage small. Router work, transfer bandwidth, cache misses, host memory, optimizer state, and recurrent applications remain real costs. Top-k per application is not necessarily top-k distinct experts per generated token when a block repeats.

Another inference requiring testing: selecting a resident expert set using requests aggregated across a training window could create a future-information path unless the admission protocol is prefix-causal. This review did not execute a leakage test or establish a defect. MLM must test prefix invariance for routing and paging as well as attention.

### 14.3 What to borrow and what to verify

Borrow principles: stable module IDs, optimizer state attached to module identity, explicit growth events, newborn protection, separation of total capacity from resident capacity, and before/after retention probes. These are design lessons, not a proposal to copy the full implementation.

Before reproducing the second project: pin source and checkpoint revisions; inspect evaluation boundaries; compare sequential and interleaved domain schedules; retain optimizer state across restarts; separate raw decoding from repetition controls; measure storage and transfer costs; and evaluate an untouched test set. Repeated validation-driven learning-rate or growth decisions require a separate final test.

Interleaving is a meaningful baseline, but it does not logically guarantee zero forgetting. Repeatedly training all domains may still reduce some capabilities. Likewise, an unused module may hold a rare useful skill: usage alone is not sufficient justification for pruning in MLM.

| [ModuleFormer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.04640) | Sparse modules support experiments in extension and specialization | A particularly relevant novelty comparison, not proof of our graph design |
