# Binding transfer through pairing, color and wording diversity

Three hierarchical-model trials compare fixed data, a larger canonical pool, and that same larger pool with varied wording. Every arm independently starts from the preserved English-only checkpoint, not a previous QA endpoint. The graph, sum readout, split learning rates, seed 42 and batch 4/unroll 128 stay fixed. Every arm receives 2,000 QA updates plus 2,000 English rehearsal updates; all endpoints are fixed with fresh optimizers. No development-based checkpoint selection occurs.

## Data and comparison boundaries

A new seed 904217 snapshot has 16 training labels and disjoint 16-label new development/test pools. Familiar-name development and test reserve disjoint balanced matchings of 8 pairs each. A third matching covers all training names for the fixed control. Larger pools contain 32 training pairs, balanced 16 within-role/16 cross-role, and include that fixed matching. These roles are offline strata, not model inputs or neural expert labels.

Fixed uses 8 pairs × 1 color pair × 2 fact orders = 16 complete four-question groups. Diverse uses 32 pairs × 2 complementary color pairs × 2 orders = 128 groups. Mixed preserves every diverse fact, query entity, candidate list, label and group ID, but uses two fact renderers and two question renderers. The four combinations are balanced across pair/color cases, with both fact orders using the same renderer choice. No model or inference implementation changed.

| Arm | Groups | QA documents | Training names | Presentations/group | Fact/query rendering |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| fixed | 16 | 64 | 16 | 125 | canonical |
| diverse | 128 | 512 | 16 | 15–16 | canonical |
| mixed | 128 | 512 | 16 | 15–16 | four combinations of two fact/two query forms |

Fixed versus diverse tests the combined addition of partners and color coverage at a fixed update/supervision budget. It does not isolate these two diversity factors or match repetitions per example. Diverse versus mixed is a stronger paired comparison: identical sampled underlying episodes, with only rendered wording changing. Wording changes input bytes; padded batch/unroll and answer supervision remain shared. Larger-pool failure at this budget cannot establish a capacity limit. Training partner counts and sampled query frequencies are included per name in summary.json; diverse degrees/frequencies vary, whereas fixed uses one partner per name.

Development and test each contain 2,304 questions / 288 eight-condition cases in six buckets: familiar pairs versus new names, crossed with base, alternate and heldout wording. Every bucket has 48 cases across 8 pairs and six color combinations. Base rendering is trained in every arm; alternate rendering is trained only by mixed. Heldout uses a third fact and question form absent from all task-training pools. Task-level name/wording absence does not guarantee absence from English pretraining. This is narrow grammar transfer, not broad English understanding.

## Training acquisition and English retention

The joint diagnostic gate requires at least 87.5% complete training groups and English development loss ≤1.25× source. Source English development loss is 1.352696. A complete training group requires all four assignment/query conditions; test cases additionally require both sentence orders. Answer rankings use two candidate colors rather than unrestricted generation.

| Arm | Train answers correct | Complete training groups | English development loss | Source multiple | Acquisition/retention gate |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| fixed | 35/64 | 0/16 | 1.303425 | 0.964× | fails |
| diverse | 256/512 | 0/128 | 1.296879 | 0.959× | fails |
| mixed | 256/512 | 0/128 | 1.301324 | 0.962× | fails |

## Fresh locked test

All three endpoint hashes and the original English source hash were saved before any model scored the test questions. The reliable-transfer gate is at least 90% complete cases in every bucket, not merely above-chance answer accuracy. With 48 cases per bucket this requires at least 44 complete cases in each. No endpoint is promoted on this diagnostic alone.

| Checkpoint | Familiar/base | Familiar/alternate | Familiar/heldout | New/base | New/alternate | New/heldout | Complete total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| source | 0/48 | 0/48 | 0/48 | 0/48 | 0/48 | 0/48 | 0/288 |
| fixed | 0/48 | 0/48 | 0/48 | 0/48 | 0/48 | 0/48 | 0/288 |
| diverse | 0/48 | 0/48 | 0/48 | 0/48 | 0/48 | 0/48 | 0/288 |
| mixed | 0/48 | 0/48 | 0/48 | 0/48 | 0/48 | 0/48 | 0/288 |

| Checkpoint | Individual answer ranking accuracy |
|---|---:|
| source | 50.043% |
| fixed | 50.087% |
| diverse | 49.566% |
| mixed | 50.000% |

Complete eight-condition cases expose shortcuts masked by individual-answer scores. Both within/cross strata, raw likelihoods, initial/final development results and selected raw text are preserved. Raw generation covers the fixed first four questions in each of six test buckets (24 examples per trained arm), limited to 12 output bytes with no extraction or answer repair. This is not a comprehensive free-generation benchmark. Source test ranking is included without raw sampling.

## Exposure, costs and integrity

| Arm | QA payload bytes | QA supervised bytes | English payload/supervised bytes | Optimizer updates |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| fixed | 776,000 | 40,000 | 958,088 | 4000 |
| diverse | 776,000 | 40,000 | 958,088 | 4000 |
| mixed | 768,008 | 40,000 | 958,088 | 4000 |

Each arm uses the same source parameters, all 16 training names, QA update count, answer-byte supervision and English stream. Canonical/mixed QA traces match exactly at the fact/query level. Fixed-pool exposure per example is much higher. Rehearsal is explicit extra work and the corpus is the same bounded English snapshot; improved development loss is not a claim about broad chat competence. The repeatedly used English test was not reopened.

Tests independently validate rendered context/questions, queried entities, correct answer labels, complete chat text, supervised byte spans and EOS; actual per-bucket name coverage; reserved pair/name/text separation; every assignment/query/order condition; balanced roles/renderers; deterministic hashes and 128-byte input bounds. The generator is offline only. Neural inference receives textual prompts and candidates; factual metadata is used for grading, not solving. Source/training inputs and all endpoint hashes are rechecked. Architecture, optimizer and training runner were reused unchanged.

One seed, a small vocabulary, finite budgets and reused source/development knowledge restrict conclusions. The three arms were fixed before these fresh model-test results, with no sweeps. Any revised method chosen after this comparison needs another confirmation snapshot. The old QA checkpoints remain historical artifacts and were never initializers here.

## Interpretation and next gate

fixed: 0/288 complete fresh test cases; reliable-transfer criterion not met.

diverse: 0/288 complete fresh test cases; reliable-transfer criterion not met.

mixed: 0/288 complete fresh test cases; reliable-transfer criterion not met.

The diversity and wording changes did not produce complete-case transfer at this offered budget. This negative result does not show that diversity cannot help or that the graph lacks capacity: the larger pools received fewer repeats, and a longer-budget learning curve would distinguish exposure limits. Before scaling a hierarchy or asserting general comprehension, compare an explicit learned memory/readout mechanism against the preserved recurrent baseline under matched training and fresh confirmation. Separate acquisition, retention and transfer gates remain necessary.

The fresh fixed control itself fails the acquisition threshold. The previous 16-group success therefore must not be read as mastery of arbitrary 16-group tasks. This dataset changes names, pair layout, color allocation and full paired sentence-order coverage relative to that earlier subset. The mismatch cannot be attributed to any one factor from this study, and failure is not solely about transferring an already learned task.

No growing nodes, named linguistic categories, Transformer replacement, sparse efficiency or arbitrary-device result is established by this study.

## Reproduction and evidence

```sh
uv run python -m mlm.transfer_data --out data/transfer-new --seed 904217
uv run python -m mlm.plasticity_run --data data/transfer-new/mixed --config configs/plasticity-split.json --init runs/scratch-english-hierarchical-v1/best.mlm --out runs/transfer-mixed-new --groups 128 --steps 2000 --rehearsal
```

Use --groups 16 with the fixed arm, and 128 with diverse/mixed, always fresh paths. Finish and lock every endpoint before model test scoring. protocol.json includes all commands and pre-run file hashes; binding-manifest.json records pools, pairs, templates and data hashes; checkpoint-lock.json precedes test evaluation; summary.json records the audits and outcomes. Source/tests/config/lock snapshots have SHA256 hashes. Weights remain under runs/transfer-{arm}-v1/final.mlm. verification.json records the 64-test suite, strengthened data check and resolved code review.

Verification: the full 64-test regression suite passed in 159.80 seconds; the strengthened transfer-data check passed separately in 1.65 seconds. Ruff lint/format and source type checks passed after archiving. The code review has no unresolved findings.

# MLM baseline and comprehension comparison

Date: 2026-10-23. Exploratory single-seed measurements.

The graph model outperformed its message-free ablation on this small English test set. A plain GRU with approximately the same allocated parameter count performed slightly better than the graph model. This does not support claiming that the spiderweb architecture beats a standard recurrent model.

| Model | Allocated parameters | Development loss | Story test loss | Test bits/byte |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| graph | 366,722 | 1.155704 | 1.121557 | 1.615753 |
| no-messages | 366,722 | 1.192971 | 1.157398 | 1.667643 |
| gru | 368,210 | 1.136525 | 1.098890 | 1.583409 |

Loss is next-byte cross-entropy in nats, including document EOS. Lower is better. All selected checkpoints were at update 4,000. Raw metrics and unedited generations are preserved in each model subdirectory.

## Protocol and limits

Same frozen TinyStories subset: 1,000 training / 32 development / 32 local test stories, complete-document processing, byte vocabulary, batch size four, chunk length 128, seed 42, 4,000 updates, learning rate 0.001, clipping, weight decay, and AdamW settings. Selection used development loss every 500 updates. Test loss did not control training. Corpus hashes, processed payload-byte counts, and final sampler snapshots match exactly.

The graph reference is the previously completed english-v1 run. The current loader reproduced its recorded development loss exactly: 1.1557040961972767. Historical graph checkpoints remain compatible. GRU checkpoints explicitly identify their architecture and have no graph topology.

Graph: eight GRUs, width 64, degree two, one communication round. Plain GRU: one cell of width 208 without message or pooling matrices. Parameter counts differ by about 0.4%, but recurrent state differs: 512 scalars per sequence for the graph versus 208 for the GRU.

Equal allocation is not equal effective capacity or compute. Message-free ablation retains at least 102,400 matrix weights disconnected from prediction loss: 4,096 message-projection weights and 98,304 message-input weights. Weight decay can still change those unused values. The ablation tests communication together with its effective parameter paths, rather than isolating topology at identical effective capacity.

Verification jobs overlapped some training runs, and the graph reference was collected earlier. Raw timings are retained, but no controlled latency, energy, or speedup conclusion is drawn. One seed does not estimate training variance; a multi-seed study and Transformer baseline remain outstanding.

## Paired reading results

Original evaluation-only diagnostic: 12 counterfactual pairs / 24 two-choice questions. Each pair changes a fact and correct answer while holding question and choices fixed. Frozen neural likelihoods rank candidates; expected-answer keys only grade results. No answer-key leakage, keyword solver, regex solver, or hardcoded inference response is used.

| Checkpoint | Format | Item accuracy | Both-in-pair accuracy | Changed answer within pair |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Graph English | plain | 50% | 0% | 0% |
| Message-free English | plain | 50% | 0% | 0% |
| Plain GRU English | plain | 50% | 0% | 0% |
| Dialogue-adapted graph | chat | 50% | 0% | 0% |

Every model kept the same preferred candidate within each pair. A fixed preference gets 50% individual accuracy on this balanced suite. These results do not demonstrate successful counterfactual reading; they do not prove hidden states contain no contextual information. This tiny authored suite is format-dependent, not a standardized general-understanding benchmark. The dialogue checkpoint has extra training and a different format, so its row is a separate diagnostic.

Final scorer version 2 places the appropriate separator inside the prompt and length-normalizes answer bytes only. Plain prompts end in `Answer: `; chat prompts end in the assistant-marker newline. Preliminary version-1 scores that included an extra space are retained under superseded-separator-scorer. Questions and answer keys were unchanged; their SHA-256 is recorded in every final artifact. There was no result-dependent question or prompt tuning.

## Reproduce

Training commands are in [README](../../README.md). Diagnostic commands:

```sh
uv run python -m mlm.comprehension runs/english-v1/best.mlm --out results/graph-reading-new.json
uv run python -m mlm.comprehension runs/baseline-no-messages/best.mlm --out results/no-messages-reading-new.json
uv run python -m mlm.comprehension runs/baseline-gru/best.mlm --out results/gru-reading-new.json
uv run python -m mlm.comprehension runs/conversation-v1/best.mlm --format chat --out results/chat-reading-new.json
```

## Decision

Keep the graph as a research candidate and the plain GRU as a baseline. Establish multi-seed behavior and an assistant-answer training objective with fresh held-out reading tasks before adding growth. Trainable edge strengths belong in a separate controlled experiment. Rewiring, node growth, and Transformer replacement remain unproven.

results/english-chat/report.md.text:
# First real-English and conversation experiments

Date: 2026-10-23. Status: completed bounded CPU experiments, not a capable-chatbot release.

## Data and training

Source data: [TinyStories](https://huggingface.co/datasets/roneneldan/TinyStories) and [Everyday Conversations](https://huggingface.co/datasets/HuggingFaceTB/everyday-conversations-llama3.1-2k). Source attribution, licenses, byte hashes, and selection limits are in [data instructions](../../data/README.md) and [download provenance](../datasets.json).

English stage: 1,000 training stories, 32 development stories, and 32 local test stories. Conversation stage: 300 conversations plus 250 rehearsed training stories; development and test each include 32 stories and 32 conversations. All documents are traversed completely, preserving paragraphs and conversation boundaries. These are bounded first-row subsets, not representative random samples of the complete datasets. No model weights or API-generated responses were imported; MLM trained its own byte prediction weights from scratch, followed by parameter-only initialization for stage two.

Architecture: eight independent GRU nodes, width 64, degree two, one synchronous message round per byte, **366,722 parameters**. Batch size four, chunk length 128. State carries across chunks; gradients are detached between chunks. Padding does not update state. Parameters remain fixed during inference; structural growth is disabled.

English training: 4,000 AdamW updates at learning rate 0.001. Dialogue adaptation: 2,000 updates at 0.0003, with a new optimizer and stream initialized from the English best parameters. The dialogue objective predicts all turns; it is not assistant-only supervised loss. Each stage uses seed 42. No hyperparameter search or multi-seed study was performed.

## Measured results

Loss is next-byte cross-entropy in nats, including EOS. Lower is better. Development data selects checkpoints; final local test data does not control training.

| Metric | Before stage | Selected checkpoint |
|---|---:|---:|
| English development loss | 6.007100 | 1.155704 |
| Mixed development loss during adaptation | 2.024821 | 1.222799 |

| Local test domain | English checkpoint | Adapted checkpoint |
|---|---:|---:|
| Stories: loss | 1.121557 | 1.108754 |
| Conversations: loss | 2.784249 | 1.361218 |
| Stories: bits/byte | 1.615753 | 1.596149 |
| Conversations: bits/byte | 4.012230 | 1.962674 |

Story prediction did not degrade in this particular rehearsal experiment. This does not establish that forgetting is solved: there is no no-rehearsal control, new-domain growth experiment, or multi-seed estimate. The same small local story test is used before/after adaptation for a planned retention comparison, rather than as a sequence of tuning signals.

## Actual chat behavior

The trained role wrapper answers `Hi!` with `Hello! How can I help you today?`. Raw generation then attempts to invent a following user turn. The single-turn CLI cuts at a new user marker; raw samples retain everything for inspection.

The probes `What is your name?`, `What color is the sky?`, and `A cat says meow. What animal says meow?` produced repetitive, irrelevant continuations. **The model does not yet demonstrate reliable question answering or comprehension.** It learned useful byte/word patterns and a greeting format. A low next-byte loss is not sufficient evidence of understanding.

See [unedited probes](chat-probes.json), [English generations](english/samples.json), and [adapted generations](conversation/samples.json). These are qualitative observations, not a standardized benchmark. Greedy decoding, no repetition penalties, at most 160 continuation bytes. No favorable samples were selected from repeated stochastic draws.

## Compute and artifacts

English training loop: 290.6 seconds, with 276.4 synchronized update seconds and 1,916,320 payload bytes processed. Dialogue loop: 171.4 seconds, with 157.4 update seconds and 946,437 payload bytes. Compilation, initial/final evaluations, and sample generation are outside loop timing. Timing includes contention from verification processes and is not a controlled performance benchmark.

Local checkpoints: `runs/english-v1/best.mlm` and `runs/conversation-v1/best.mlm`, each with a separate latest checkpoint for exact resume. JSON metrics, source fingerprints, configs, and samples are preserved here. The checkpoint contains sampler RNG/order/offsets, recurrent carry, optimizer moments, topology, and parameters.

## Reproduce and use

See [README](../../README.md) for data preparation and exact commands. Try the already trained model:

```sh
uv run mlm chat runs/conversation-v1/best.mlm --message 'Hi!'
uv run mlm generate runs/english-v1/best.mlm --prompt 'Once upon a time' --max-bytes 160
uv run mlm evaluate runs/conversation-v1/best.mlm --data data/hf/conversation/test.jsonl --full-documents
```

## Next decisions

Run matched plain-GRU, graph-without-messages, and Transformer baselines before crediting graph topology. Then test larger parameter/data budgets, assistant-only dialogue loss, and a defined comprehension/QA evaluation. A larger or longer run should be justified by those experiments, not by assuming that more data automatically fixes the architecture. Growth and rewiring remain separate research stages.

results/from-scratch/report.md.text:
# From-scratch dense versus hierarchical study

This study removes inherited-weight mismatch from the previous routing pilot. Both architectures are independently initialized for English training rather than loading a dense-trained English checkpoint into the altered recurrent update rule. The graph, sum readout, byte vocabulary, eight width64 GRUs and base initialization seed remain shared. Hierarchical routing retains its additional 1,548 parameters and auxiliary balance loss; the comparison is token/update matched, not exactly parameter/compute matched.

## Phases and boundaries

1. A separate training-only learnability probe initializes each architecture randomly at seed 42, LR 0.003, batch 4/unroll 128. It trains one existing four-question group for 500 updates, then four groups for 500 further updates with continuous optimizer state. These are memorization diagnostics; their weights never seed English pretraining or the final evaluation models.
2. Each English model is independently reset to random seed 42 and trained for 4,000 updates on the same cached 1,000 English training stories with 32 development stories, LR 0.001, batch 4/unroll 128. Full-document state carries across chunks with truncated backpropagation, and padding/document resets follow the tested streaming implementation. Minimum pure English development loss selects initial or 500-step endpoints. Only hierarchical gradients include the existing routing auxiliary; selection/evaluation losses exclude it.
3. Each architecture adapts its own development-selected English checkpoint using fresh optimizer,1,000 complete-group QA updates interleaved with 1,000 English-stream updates, LR 0.001, batch 4/unroll 128. The fresh balanced task uses seed 631204, 32 training labels, disjoint familiar-name held-out pairings, and separate 16-name new development/test pools. Both arms receive identical streams and the same adaptation budget. Primary selection maximizes macro eight-condition development correctness across known/new-name buckets; QA loss breaks ties, initial eligible. English is monitored separately, without a retention feasibility constraint in this study.
4. Both English-selected and task-selected checkpoints are locked before the fresh task and reused English tests. Additional neutral-filler test probes insert exactly 64 or 128 bytes between facts and question, without delayed-example training. They retain the same ground-truth facts and all eight assignment/query/sentence-order conditions. Zero-delay failure limits interpretation of delayed failure; it cannot by itself isolate forgetting.
5. After all training/evaluation workers finish, selected English checkpoints are measured sequentially in fresh CPU processes. Timings cover warmed JIT full forwards at batch 1 and lengths 32/128/512 with fixed seeded inputs, 5 warmups and 30 repetitions. Compilation/first execution is separate. These are not text-processing/generation latency, sparse kernels, Transformer or device-portability benchmarks. Tensor sizes and peak RSS are recorded, with RSS explicitly including checkpoint optimizer loading, JAX and compilation overhead.

All dataset/config/core-code hashes are frozen before training. No probe weights, QA data or test outcomes influence English initialization/selection. Shared base tensors must match between the two random initial checkpoints, with only router extras in hierarchical. Full stream traces and input-byte counts must match at the end of each paired training phase. Offered budgets match; development-selected step counts can differ and are reported.

## Scope

The English source is a small bounded public-data snapshot, not a full language-model corpus. Binding uses one sentence grammar and four colors, with role-balanced partitions and artificial names. Names are held out within this task, not guaranteed globally unseen. This is one seed. Source architecture pretraining mismatch is addressed, but learning rate, balance loss, model size and limited optimization budgets still restrict conclusions about architecture potential. No growing categories, verb/pronoun specialization or online inference-time weight learning is implemented.

A Transformer benchmark is a later conditional milestone. This internal comparison cannot establish replacement, superiority, broad English conversation or scaling. Useful language/retrieval performance must first be demonstrated, and later direct matched comparisons would need their own protocol and untouched confirmation sets.

## Reproduction

Use fresh output paths. The learnability probe uses the existing gradual-v1 training fixture; it never supplies pretraining weights.

```sh
uv run python -m mlm.learnability_run --config configs/scratch-probe-hierarchical.json --out runs/scratch-probe-hierarchical-new
uv run python -m mlm.pretrain_run --config configs/scratch-hierarchical.json --out runs/scratch-english-hierarchical-new --steps 4000 --eval-every 500
```

Repeat with the dense configs and fresh paths. Adapt each English best checkpoint using hierarchy_run with the fresh scratch-binding-v1 data, not another architecture's weights. Freeze both selections before tests. Full measured commands and artifact pointers accompany the results below.

## Measured results

Both pretraining runs completed 4,000 updates and 1,916,320 payload bytes. Checkpoint selection chose step 4,000 for both. Shared base initial tensors match exactly; hierarchical adds1,548 router parameters. Both adaptation runs completed 1,000 QA and 1,000 English updates with a fresh optimizer. Full sampler snapshots and update/byte accounting match between arms; checkpoint locks precede test evaluation. See `initialization-audit.json`, `stream-audit.json`, `checkpoint-lock.json`, `protocol.json` and `summary.json`.

| Model | Parameters | English selected step | English test loss | Adapt selected QA step | Adapt English test loss | Complete binding cases | Answer ranking accuracy |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| dense | 366,722 | 4000 | 1.121557 | 1000 | 1.126128 | 0/144 | 50.347% |
| hierarchical | 368,270 | 4000 | 1.323535 | 750 | 1.321262 | 0/144 | 50.000% |

Lower English loss is better. These losses are pure next-byte cross-entropy including document EOS; no routing auxiliary is included. The repeatedly used 32-story English test is a retention diagnostic, not an untouched broad-language confirmation. Adaptation selection has no English-retention constraint.

### Memorization sanity

| Model | One training group,500 updates | Four groups, 500 further updates | Fixed first-group greedy samples after four-group stage |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| dense | 100.0% | 62.5% | 50.0% |
| hierarchical | 100.0% | 100.0% | 100.0% |

Ranking covers 4/16 training questions respectively; greedy samples cover the fixed first four questions only, without extraction or answer repair. Probe weights never initialize either English run. This establishes finite-budget memorization, not generalization or broad language understanding. Probe random initialization matches the separately saved English initial base tensors at the same seed. No initial probe ranking was recorded; this reporting omission does not change pretraining initialization or selection.

### Fresh binding and neutral delays

| Model | Delay bytes | Familiar names, new pairs | New names | Complete total | Answer ranking accuracy |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| dense | 0 | 0/96 | 0/48 | 0/144 | 50.347% |
| dense | 64 | 0/96 | 0/48 | 0/144 | 50.000% |
| dense | 128 | 0/96 | 0/48 | 0/144 | 50.000% |
| hierarchical | 0 | 0/96 | 0/48 | 0/144 | 50.000% |
| hierarchical | 64 | 0/96 | 0/48 | 0/144 | 50.000% |
| hierarchical | 128 | 0/96 | 0/48 | 0/144 | 49.913% |

Each complete case requires all eight color-assignment, query and sentence-order conditions. Familiar/new buckets contain 96/48 cases; within/cross role strata are balanced and reported in each test artifact. Candidate scoring uses only prompts and candidate strings; correct indices and fact metadata grade outputs offline. Greedy answers from fixed zero-delay groups are also preserved. Delays were never trained or used for selection. If zero-delay binding fails, delayed failures cannot isolate additional forgetting. All conditions share a narrow grammar and four colors; this is one seed.

### CPU forward timing and storage

| Model | Length | Warmed median ms | p95 ms | Compile + first forward seconds |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| dense | 32 | 0.817 | 1.047 | 0.132 |
| dense | 128 | 3.321 | 4.116 | 0.147 |
| dense | 512 | 13.054 | 14.665 | 0.178 |
| hierarchical | 32 | 0.823 | 1.047 | 0.169 |
| hierarchical | 128 | 3.338 | 3.708 | 0.166 |
| hierarchical | 512 | 13.557 | 14.461 | 0.181 |

| Model | Float parameter bytes | Optimizer tensor bytes | Persistent state bytes/sequence | Peak process RSS KiB |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| dense | 1,466,888 | 2,933,780 | 2,048 | 349,832 |
| hierarchical | 1,473,080 | 2,946,164 | 2,048 | 363,272 |

Separate processes ran sequentially after training/evaluation, using the same fixed random byte inputs, batch 1, five warmups and 30 timed forwards. Peak RSS includes optimizer checkpoint loading, JAX and compilation; it is not isolated inference RAM. Dense execution computes all nodes in both models. These timings do not measure generation loops, sparse dispatch, a Transformer comparison or arbitrary-device deployment. Training wall times were concurrent and are not a controlled training-speed comparison.

### Interpretation and next gate

Neither selected model demonstrates robust binding on this fresh test. Removing inherited-weight mismatch allowed independent English learning, but does not establish that hierarchical routing improves language modeling or solves binding. The hierarchical model can memorize a small training set, so a categorical claim that the architecture cannot learn is also unsupported. The next controlled step is to locate acquisition failure with nested training-set sizes and training-versus-held-out swap scores under a fixed own-architecture source, before adding categories, growth or expert depth. Reserve fresh confirmation data for any revised algorithm. No Transformer replacement, chatbot readiness or general efficiency claim follows from this study.

All 56 regression tests passed (167.76 seconds); Ruff, formatting and source type checks passed. Current source/tests/configuration/lockfile are snapshotted under `code/` with SHA256 hashes. `execution-script.py.txt` records the local orchestration; direct CLI commands above are preferable for fresh output paths. No architecture or default-checkpoint changes were made in this study.

results/from-scratch/protocol.md.text:
# From-scratch dense versus hierarchical study

Approved next step: check hierarchical learnability, pretrain both architectures fairly on English, then evaluate binding/retention/runtime before considering a Transformer baseline. Keep architecture and routing unchanged.

Two modes only: dense and hierarchical, eight width64 GRUs, fixed graph/sum readout, four groups/two children for routing, seed42. Shared base parameter initializations match exactly; hierarchical has its existing 1,548 router parameters and balance coefficient0.01. Soft execution remains dense. This is token/update matched, not exactly parameter/compute matched.

1. Training-only learnability probe: fresh random state for each mode, LR0.003, batch4/unroll128. Train the first existing gradual-data group for500 updates, then first four groups for500 additional updates, carrying optimizer state. Record initial/500/1000 train ranking and fixed raw samples. No held-out claim, checkpoint selection or source transfer into pretraining. Failure at this finite budget is not an architecture impossibility result.
2. Independently initialize both modes again from seed42; do not load probe weights. English full-document pretraining: same cached1000 train/32 development stories, LR0.001, batch4/unroll128, 4,000 updates and development evaluation every500. Include routing auxiliary only in hierarchical gradient objective; language evaluation remains pure cross-entropy. Select minimum English development loss with initial eligible. Save initial/latest/best, optimizer and stream/carry provenance. Dedicated driver is fresh-only, not a resume implementation.
3. Fresh balanced binding data seed631204 (same verified confirmation generator). Train each mode from its own development-selected English checkpoint using hierarchy_run, fresh optimizer, 1,000 QA +1,000 English updates, evaluate every250 QA cycles. Same task/English streams, LR0.001. Select macro eight-condition known/new-name development correctness, then pure QA loss, initial eligible. English monitored separately. No warm-start mismatch between update modes.
4. Freeze/check hashes and lock both English and task-selected checkpoints before test. Score English pretraining and adapted English retention, fresh known/new-name binding with zero filler, and separate64/128-byte neutral-filler test probes (same fact assignments, no delayed training). Require all eight conditions including sentence order. Delayed failure cannot diagnose extra forgetting if zero-delay binding already fails. These are one-seed shared-grammar diagnostics, not chat competence.
5. After training ends, benchmark selected English models sequentially in fresh processes: warmed JIT forward pass, batch1, lengths32/128/512, 5 warmups and30 timed repetitions; compile time reported separately. Report parameter and optimizer tensor bytes, persistent recurrent state bytes, and peak process RSS including JAX/compilation overhead. Timings exclude text I/O and are not generation latency, sparse dispatch, Transformer, device-portability or scaling evidence. Fixed seeded inputs and environment are recorded.

Tests: fresh-only driver/output guards, no supervised-span misuse, source and initial shared-weight identity, stream coverage/steps/counters, selected checkpoint, finite routed updates and runtime artifact schema smoke. Reuse existing routing/binding/evaluation tests. Freeze configs/data/source/code before relevant phases. Preserve prior source/checkpoints; save all negative outcomes and update research/PRD/README. No sweeps or test-based model choices. A direct Transformer comparison remains unjustified unless useful capabilities are demonstrated; this study cannot establish replacement.

results/hierarchical-routing/report.md.text:
# Hierarchical recurrent update routing

This is a two-level learned update-routing prototype inside the existing eight-node recurrent graph, not a completed growing or grammar-labelled architecture. Four router groups contain two independent GRU subnetworks each. There are no assigned verb/pronoun experts, symbolic question parser, inference answer rules, learned edges or node growth. A source snapshot is preserved under code/ with hashes for reproducibility as the workspace evolves.

## Mechanism

At each byte, concatenate its learned embedding with the mean previous node state. A root softmax predicts four group probabilities; group-specific child softmaxes predict probabilities for the two nodes inside each group. Their product p_i is a normalized distribution over eight recurrent nodes. Within each synchronous GRU round:

h_i(new) = h_i(old) + p_i * (GRU_i(input, messages, h_i(old)) - h_i(old)).

Gates use only current/past input and respect document resets. Padding preserves state and contributes no routing mass. Soft probabilities normally give every node a partial update; unselected states are not literally frozen as they would be under a hard sparse gate. This prototype therefore tests learned multirate memory updates, not actual sparse execution.

The bounded directed message graph and sum readout remain unchanged. Grouping is an organizational routing hierarchy; internal/cross-group rewiring or separate parent memories are not added. Each child is itself a small neural network with its own GRU parameters. Category specialization would require subsequent probing/data and is not demonstrated by module names or routing probabilities.

Hierarchical routing is established prior art in [sparsely gated/hierarchical MoE research](https://arxiv.org/html/1701.06538v1). This particular recurrent state-update adaptation is a hypothesis to test, not a claim that nesting experts is a newly discovered neural principle.

## Controls and training

Three arms share the same eight width-64 GRUs, 512-float recurrent state, source English weights, data, seed and budget:

- Dense: every node uses its ordinary GRU update (nominal gate mass eight).
- Uniform slow: every node blends at p_i=1/8 (nominal gate mass one).
- Hierarchical: learned group/child probabilities, also total gate mass one.

The fixed-slow arm isolates slowing memory from learning a router. Both router layers start at zero, so hierarchical and uniform models initially match exactly after shared-weight transfer. They do not initially reproduce the dense English model's behavior: changing the update timescale changes the recurrent computation. Initial English/QA losses must therefore be reported, not treated as equivalent initial predictions.

Hierarchical adds 1,548 parameters (368,270 total); controls each have 366,722. The parameter/state distinction is explicit; this is not an exactly parameter-matched test. Existing defaults remain dense and legacy checkpoints load. Ordinary stream warm starts reject update-mode mismatch, while the experimental initializer copies shared tensors and initializes the new router parameters.

The hierarchical training objective adds 0.01*(N*sum(mean_route_probability_i^2)-1), with valid input positions only and zero penalty for empty batches. This encourages balanced usage; it does not guarantee specialization or correct routing. Reported language loss and checkpoint tiebreaks exclude the auxiliary penalty. Usage/entropy diagnostics are accumulated over training positions; dense/uniform reference probabilities are uniform, while their actual nominal update masses differ.

Fresh role-balanced data use generator seed 920231, separate from the previous test snapshot. There are 32 training labels, 16 new development and 16 new test labels; within/cross-role pair counts are balanced. Each arm starts from runs/english-v1/best.mlm with fresh optimizer, seed42, LR0.001, batch4, unroll128. Each receives 1,000 QA-group updates and 1,000 explicit English streaming updates, with independent recurrent carry for English. Model selection at initial and every250 QA cycles maximizes macro eight-condition development correctness across familiar/new-name pools, then minimizes pure QA loss; ties keep earlier weights. English development is monitored, not a feasibility constraint in this experiment. best.mlm here is therefore not the English-protected policy of the previous runner.

Data/config/source/model/runner hashes are frozen before training. All three selected hashes must be locked before the fresh task and English tests are scored. There is no sweep or Transformer baseline. These models still compute every node; no sparse speedup follows. Runtime under shared CPU contention is not a controlled benchmark.

## Reproduction

Use fresh paths. Preserve the source checkpoint and cached English data.

```sh
uv run python -m mlm.confirmation_data --out data/hierarchy-new --seed 920231
uv run python -m mlm.hierarchy_run --data data/hierarchy-new --config configs/hierarchy-hierarchical.json --init runs/english-v1/best.mlm --out runs/hierarchy-new --steps 1000 --eval-every 250
uv run python -m mlm.gradual_eval runs/hierarchy-new/best.mlm --questions data/hierarchy-new/test-questions.json --out results/hierarchy-new-test.json
```

Repeat training with hierarchy-dense.json and hierarchy-uniform.json under fresh output names, then lock all selected checkpoints before testing. The runner has no resume feature. The preserved source snapshot can be placed on PYTHONPATH via code/src when reproducing this exact implementation. Current experiment files and hashes identify which code/config/data were used.

## Transformer replacement standard

The [Transformer paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762) establishes an attention-based architecture with empirical sequence-task results. This prototype has not been compared directly with a Transformer under matched data and resource budgets. A replacement claim would need competitive held-out language quality and retrieval, controlled training/inference cost, memory/device measurements, longer-context tests and scaling across seeds/model sizes. Small synthetic successes, parameter counts, or a visually brain-like hierarchy do not meet that standard.

## Measured results

All three arms completed 1,000 QA plus 1,000 English updates. Each consumed exactly 388,000 QA input bytes / 20,000 supervised QA payload bytes, and 479,511 English input/supervised payload bytes. QA/English sampler traces match; only state-update mechanism and router parameters/objective differ. Source/config/data/runner hashes were verified and all three selected checkpoint hashes locked before test.

All development primary binding scores remain zero, so the pure QA-loss tiebreak selects dense QA step1,000, uniform step750, and hierarchical step1,000. The uniform test result is therefore for its earlier selected checkpoint, not its final state.

| Variant | Parameters | Selected QA step | Familiar-name cases /96 | New-name cases /48 | English test loss | QA test loss |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Dense updates | 366,722 | 1,000 | 0 | 0 | 1.119035 | 0.235698 |
| Fixed slow updates | 366,722 | 750 | 0 | 0 | 1.953038 | 0.174190 |
| Hierarchical learned updates | 368,270 | 1,000 | 0 | 0 | 1.473429 | 0.159689 |

Each case requires all eight assignment/query/sentence-order predictions correct. All within/cross-role test strata also have zero complete cases. Individual two-choice accuracy is 49.74%, 50.52%, and 50.87%. Lower QA byte loss does not demonstrate binding: formatting and teacher-forced word completion can improve without reliable query-dependent retrieval.

Learned routing improves English prediction relative to the fixed-slow control in this pilot, but remains worse than dense updates. There is no demonstrated binding benefit. These are one-seed selected-checkpoint results, not statistical or scaling conclusions. The unchanged source English reference has story-test loss 1.121557; the repeated story set is a retention monitor, not a fresh broad language benchmark.

Raw greedy samples are stored separately for the fixed first full group from each of two pools (eight samples per model), with whitespace/case normalization only. They are not full-test generation scores. All item likelihoods and errors remain in the JSON evidence.

## Router activity and limits

Both router layers changed from zero: root-kernel L2 norm is about 5.83, child-kernel 5.28, with nonzero biases. The actual soft router trained, rather than staying a fixed uniform mask. Cumulative QA mean usage is approximately [0.088, 0.096, 0.187, 0.206, 0.100, 0.094, 0.122, 0.107]. English usage is approximately [0.043, 0.038, 0.104, 0.542, 0.037, 0.031, 0.143, 0.061].

This shows input/domain-dependent utilization, not verified linguistic expertise. English traffic concentrates in node3 despite the auxiliary balance penalty. Balanced usage is encouraged, not guaranteed; entropy and mean batch penalty are saved to make this visible. No verbs/pronouns/nouns categories were assigned or demonstrated.

Algebraically, if the original GRU retention gate is z_i, the outer update gate gives an effective retention coefficient 1-p_i*(1-z_i). This parameterizes memory timescales and couples node updates through a global learned router. It is not evidence of an entirely new learning principle. The router uses a global pooled previous state, so disabling explicit neighbor messages would still leave this global routing path; a future message ablation must account for it.

The controls isolate dense versus uniformly slowed versus learned slowed updates, but do not isolate hierarchical factorization from an ordinary flat learned gate. A flat learned-router control remains outstanding before claiming that hierarchy specifically adds value. The hierarchical arm also has extra parameters and a balancing auxiliary; their contributions are not independently separated.

A major initialization limitation is that all shared weights came from a dense-trained English model. Uniform/hierarchical initial English development loss is 3.770138, versus dense 1.155704. Hierarchical and uniform match each other initially exactly, but neither is function-equivalent to the dense source. This is a warm-start adaptation pilot, not a fair from-scratch assessment of each architecture's best language-model potential. Adequate matched pretraining would be needed for that stronger comparison.

## Decision

The first two-level routing implementation is functional and testable, but it has not solved the current learning failure. It is not adopted as the default English/chat model. Default dense behavior and earlier checkpoints remain preserved. There is no node growth, arbitrary-depth category tree, sparse kernel dispatch, online weight learning, or Transformer-replacement evidence.

All 54 tests passed, plus Ruff and type checks. Tests include legacy behavior, normalized/factored routes, fixed-slow equivalence, exact blend math, nonzero router gradients, context dependence, causality, resets, padding, chunk state, checkpoint replay, empty-batch optimizer safety, and an end-to-end routed training run. Source snapshots and hashes preserve this implementation for future review.

Further work should distinguish learned flat gating from hierarchical gating, address pretraining mismatch, and demonstrate actual retrieval before increasing depth or expert count. Hard routing/dispatch and Transformer baselines require separate quality/cost experiments. A model hierarchy that resembles a brain or web is an engineering hypothesis, not proof of intelligence or an automatic successor to Transformers.

results/hierarchical-routing/protocol.md.text:
# Hierarchical recurrent update routing prototype

Authorized: prototype four groups of two small recurrent networks, compare with the current graph, and assess whether evidence supports a Transformer replacement. Current answer: no replacement claim; no direct Transformer baseline, broad language benchmark, scaling study or controlled device runtime evidence exists.

Keep all eight GRUs, width 64, fixed bounded message graph and sum readout. Add config node_update=dense|uniform|hierarchical (default dense), groups=4, router_balance=0.01. Hierarchical root gate selects group probabilities and conditional child gates select node probabilities from current byte embedding concatenated with mean previous node state. Their product is a distribution over eight nodes. Within each GRU round blend h_new = p_i*GRU_candidate + (1-p_i)*h_old. Fixed-uniform control uses p_i=1/8; dense uses p_i=1. This distinguishes learned routing from simply slowing memory updates. There are no assigned grammar categories, POS parser, inference label lookup, dynamic growth or learned topology. Existing graph supplies bounded within/cross connections; changing topology is deliberately excluded from this first test.

Both router layers start with zero weights/biases, so hierarchical and uniform controls initially match exactly after copying shared parameters. Root/child parameters must receive finite nonzero gradients. Hierarchical adds 1,548 parameters at width64/groups4/nodes8; memory state remains 512 floats. Soft routing still computes all nodes and cannot establish sparse speed gains. Auxiliary balance loss is 0.01*(N*sum(mean_probability_i^2)-1), with padding excluded; mean routing usage/entropy and write mass are reported separately from byte prediction loss. This encourages balanced usage but does not prove useful specialization.

Preserve legacy defaults, forward/checkpoint/generation interfaces; optional return_routes=True exposes route probabilities only for this trainer/diagnostics. Test probability normalization, two-level factorization, uniform equivalence, partial memory retention, causality, resets/padding/chunk equivalence, gradients, parameter delta, default checkpoints and config validation. Standard stream warm starts must reject update-mode mismatches; experimental warm-start copies shared weights and initializes router extras.

Fresh role-balanced data via confirmation_data seed override 920231; old default seed unchanged. Same English source runs/english-v1/best.mlm for all three arms, fresh optimizers, LR0.001, batch4, unroll128. Each arm receives 1,000 QA updates plus 1,000 explicit English updates, identical QA/English stream order, evaluation every250 QA cycles. Same data, budget and base parameters; initial inference differs with update rate. No English feasibility constraint is inherited from the last study: select only by macro eight-condition known/new-name development accuracy, then QA development loss, exact ties earlier. English dev monitored separately, source reference recorded. Initial eligible. No sweeps/resume. Auxiliary balance is training-only; language metrics remain pure prediction loss.

Freeze source/config/data/code hashes before training; lock all selected hashes before fresh test. Evaluate balanced known/new-name, within/cross, both sentence orders, English retention and route utilization. Store all negative results. Runtime is uncontrolled, soft routing dense, parameters unequal: no replacement, speed, memory-efficiency or superiority claim. Cite established hierarchical MoE rather than claiming its principle is novel. Update research, PRD and usage after measured results.

# Binding acquisition at increasing dataset sizes

This exploratory diagnostic keeps the recurrent graph and routing unchanged. Each mode independently starts four trials from its own frozen from-scratch English best checkpoint, using fresh optimizer state, learning rate 0.003, seed 42 and exactly 500 task updates. Nested 1/4/16/64-group subsets are prefixes of one seeded permutation of the 256-group training pool. A group contains all four assignment/query swaps for one fact order. Groups are sampled in shuffled cycles; endpoints are fixed and no best checkpoint is selected. No held-out test data is opened.

This is task-only training, with no English rehearsal, to isolate acquisition. Learning rate and rehearsal differ from the previous joint-training study, so cross-study changes cannot be attributed to subset size alone. Within this study, paired modes have identical subset identities, update traces, input bytes and supervision bytes. Each mode's starting parameter hash is identical across its four trials, optimizer step starts at zero, and source checkpoint hashes remain unchanged.

## Results

Train questions are ranked by neural likelihood over two candidate colors. Complete training groups require all four answers correct; development cases require all eight conditions including both fact orders. English loss is measured on the same 32 development stories before and after each trial. This is a diagnostic development set, not a final confirmation.

| Model | Training groups | Unique names | Train answers correct | Complete train groups | Familiar-pool dev cases | New-pool dev cases | English dev loss before → after |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| dense | 1 | 2 | 4/4 | 1/1 | 0/96 | 0/48 | 1.156 → 6.499 |
| dense | 4 | 8 | 16/16 | 4/4 | 0/96 | 0/48 | 1.156 → 5.587 |
| dense | 16 | 26 | 32/64 | 0/16 | 0/96 | 0/48 | 1.156 → 5.210 |
| dense | 64 | 32 | 128/256 | 0/64 | 0/96 | 0/48 | 1.156 → 4.414 |
| hierarchical | 1 | 2 | 4/4 | 1/1 | 0/96 | 0/48 | 1.353 → 5.319 |
| hierarchical | 4 | 8 | 16/16 | 4/4 | 0/96 | 0/48 | 1.353 → 6.798 |
| hierarchical | 16 | 26 | 36/64 | 1/16 | 0/96 | 0/48 | 1.353 → 4.981 |
| hierarchical | 64 | 32 | 128/256 | 0/64 | 0/96 | 0/48 | 1.353 → 5.591 |

## Name coverage and interpretation

The original familiar-name bucket refers to the full 32-name training pool. Small subsets contain fewer names, so many familiar-pool development questions actually contain unseen task labels for that trial. No development pair is a training pair. The following breakdown counts how many of each case's two names occur in the actual trial subset; all conditions for each case stay together. Zero means both names absent, one means mixed coverage, and two means both seen in some training groups. Labels may have occurred in English pretraining; task absence does not guarantee global novelty.

| Model | Training groups | Zero seen names, complete dev cases | One seen name | Two seen names |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| dense | 1 | 0/132 | 0/12 | 0/0 |
| dense | 4 | 0/102 | 0/36 | 0/6 |
| dense | 16 | 0/60 | 0/12 | 0/72 |
| dense | 64 | 0/48 | 0/0 | 0/96 |
| hierarchical | 1 | 0/132 | 0/12 | 0/0 |
| hierarchical | 4 | 0/102 | 0/36 | 0/6 |
| hierarchical | 16 | 0/60 | 0/12 | 0/72 |
| hierarchical | 64 | 0/48 | 0/0 | 0/96 |

Four independent starting points prevent earlier small-set optimization from receiving extra credit at larger sizes. Fixed 500-update budgets imply approximately 500, 125, 31 or 8 presentations per group respectively. Declining training fit can reflect optimization/sample exposure as well as interference or capacity; this study cannot distinguish these causes or prove an architectural limit. Shared grammar, four color words, one seed and the same exploratory development data limit generalization claims. Eight-condition success is stricter than a chance-level single-answer score; both metrics are retained in the raw artifacts.

Each summary includes initial/final training and development metrics, fixed first-training-group raw generations without answer repair, unique name/pair/color coverage, byte counters and all 500 sampled group IDs. Correct labels and fact metadata are offline graders; the network receives textual prompts and candidate answer strings. No category solver, regex answer extraction, growth or extra expert machinery was added.

## Next decision

dense: completely fits training groups at tested sizes [1, 4]. hierarchical: completely fits training groups at tested sizes [1, 4]. 

Training fit and development transfer are separate gates. Before increasing model complexity, the next comparison should control presentations per example and test whether learning interference or insufficient repetitions explains larger-set failures. Any curriculum should be compared with a flat control at matched total updates. English retention must be restored explicitly before promoting a checkpoint; these task-only endpoints do not replace the preserved English models. Revised training choices require fresh confirmation data. This study provides no Transformer superiority, dynamic-growth or chatbot-readiness evidence.

## Reproduction and evidence

```sh
uv run python -m mlm.acquisition_run --config configs/acquisition-dense.json --init runs/scratch-english-dense-v1/best.mlm --out runs/acquisition-dense-new
uv run python -m mlm.acquisition_run --config configs/acquisition-hierarchical.json --init runs/scratch-english-hierarchical-v1/best.mlm --out runs/acquisition-hierarchical-new
```

Use fresh output paths. The runner is fresh-only, with no resume support. `protocol.json` freezes code/config/data/source hashes; `summary.json` includes paired audit results and endpoint checkpoint hashes. Architecture-specific sources differ because each was trained in its own mode; this is a paired pipeline comparison, not a single-tensor gate ablation. Raw scores are archived per mode/subset, and source/tests/configs/lockfile snapshots have separate SHA256 hashes. Local weights remain under runs/acquisition-{mode}-v1/groups-{N}/final.mlm.

Verification: all 58 regression tests passed in 176.44 seconds. Ruff lint/format and source type checks passed. The two new safeguard tests first failed because the diagnostic module was absent, then passed with the implementation.

# MLM v0.1 CPU smoke result

Run date: 2026-10-23. This is an engineering smoke experiment, not a language capability benchmark.

- Architecture: 8 independent GRU modules, width 32, two incoming edges, one synchronous round per byte.
- Parameters: 100,546.
- Data: 36 original template sentences for training; 18 different sentences for development. Grammar overlaps deliberately; some development words are unseen. No document was truncated. No independent final test was used.
- Optimizer: clipped AdamW, learning rate 0.003, batch size 4, unroll 64, seed 42.
- Updates: 300; development evaluation every 50 updates.
- Backend: CPU; exact versions and source digest are in environment.json and uv.lock.

| Metric | Before training | Final step 300 |
|---|---:|---:|
| Training next-token loss, nats, including EOS | 6.129411 | 0.205798 |
| Development next-token loss, nats, including EOS | 6.091121 | 2.046138 |
| Development payload bits/byte | 8.734793 | 3.099455 |

Best evaluated development checkpoint: step 50, loss 1.653910. Its greedy continuation of `The ` was `red cat rests.`. A continuation of `The red bird` was ` rests.`. Full decoding metadata is in samples.json.

Development loss worsened after step 50 despite continued low training loss. The run exhibits overfitting; best.mlm preserves the best evaluated checkpoint, while latest.mlm preserves the resumable latest state.

Measured training-loop time: 7.323 seconds, including periodic evaluation and checkpoint saves but excluding initial evaluation, training-step compilation, final evaluation, and sample generation. Training-step compilation took 1.135 seconds. Synchronized updates took 4.359 seconds, processing 23,101 payload bytes at about 5299 bytes/second. This is training throughput, not generation speed. Peak process RSS was 418.1 MiB; it includes the Python/JAX process and is not just model memory. The latest resumable checkpoint was 1,208,492 bytes.

## Interpretation

The code learns a tiny text distribution, runs causal graph computation, generates continuations, and can resume training exactly in the tested environment. It does not establish better quality or efficiency than a Transformer or a GRU. There is one seed, a tiny synthetic corpus, no matched baseline, no independent final test, and no capacity growth.

## Reproduce

```sh
uv sync --locked
uv run mlm train --train data/smoke/train.txt --validation data/smoke/validation.txt --config configs/smoke.json --out runs/reproduction --steps 300 --eval-every 50
uv run mlm generate runs/reproduction/best.mlm --prompt 'The ' --max-bytes 64
uv run mlm evaluate runs/reproduction/best.mlm --data data/smoke/validation.txt
```

Use an unused output directory. The source fingerprint in environment.json describes this run's source. Numerical and runtime variation across machines and package/backend versions is expected. Checkpoints are local under runs/smoke-reviewed; text/JSON run evidence is copied here. The earlier runs/smoke experiment preceded a bias-decay correction and is not the result reported in this table.

results/gradual-binding/report.md.text:
# Gradual binding versus a matched flat control

This experiment keeps the original eight-node sum-readout graph unchanged. It starts from the separate checkpoint that memorized one four-question Dan/Ned gold/blue binding group. The source already received 500 updates on that group after its earlier English and basic-stage training. Both arms start with identical source parameters and a fresh optimizer, then receive 3,000 additional updates. The experiment does not count source-history updates as part of that new budget.

## Data and questions

The nested training pool has 64 groups / 256 questions. All groups cross two color assignments and two queried people, and each group occupies one four-example batch. First comes the exact source memorization group. The first four groups introduce eight training names; the next four reverse those fact orders. Further groups add color combinations and other entity partners. By 32 groups all 20 allowed training entity pairs appear; four other pairs are reserved for development and four for test. Exact training texts cannot appear in either evaluation split.

Evaluation has two distinct buckets, each with 48 four-question groups / 192 questions:

- New pairings of familiar training-pool names, with pair identities absent from training.
- A separate eight-name pool that does not occur in this task's training names.

Each bucket's four entity pairs cover all eight of its names, all six color pairs, and both fact orders. Development and test have different reserved familiar-name pairs and different new-name pools. Shared grammar and four color words intentionally isolate binding rather than unfamiliar wording. Names are held out within this task, not guaranteed globally unseen in English pretraining. This is a bounded synthetic task, not a broad chat benchmark.

Early familiar-name-pool development rows may include names not yet introduced for binding in the current run. Logs therefore include names sampled in the run and an additional metric restricted to genuinely sampled-name pairs. Source training history is excluded from that coverage counter. Selection only begins once all eight training names have been sampled.

## Fixed comparison

Curriculum adds groups at 500-update stages: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, then 64. The already memorized single-group checkpoint supplies the initial one-group reference. Adam state and optimizer step count continue across stages. The flat control sees all 64 groups from the start for the same total 3,000 updates, with continuous shuffling. Both use the same source, seed 42, batch four, unroll 128, learning rate 0.003, architecture, and parameter count. Learning rate matches the prior successful sanity run; it is not tuned on this test.

All examples fit one unroll, so answer loss can backpropagate to all input facts. Prompt bytes update neural state but receive no target loss. Assistant answer/newline and EOS are supervised. Recurrent state resets between independent examples/groups. There is no story rehearsal; English prediction is monitored separately and does not choose checkpoints.

Initial and 500-update scores are diagnostic only. Both arms select among update endpoints 1,000–3,000 after actual eight-name coverage, maximizing complete-group development accuracy over the fixed equal-sized familiar/new-name buckets, then minimizing target loss. Exact ties retain the earlier endpoint. The global development score therefore equals the mean of the two bucket group accuracies. Training accuracy and the reused English story diagnostic do not control selection. The runner does not support resume and refuses nonempty outputs.

Data, config, source, runner and generator hashes are frozen in protocol.json. Both selected checkpoint hashes are locked before the new test is evaluated. There is no hyperparameter sweep. Repeated experiments informed this task design, and the source is a post-hoc memorization checkpoint; findings require independent confirmation before claims of general language understanding or a robust curriculum advantage.

## Reproduction

Use fresh output paths. The seed-group artifact and sanity source checkpoint must exist.

```sh
uv run python -m mlm.gradual_data --out data/gradual-new
uv run python -m mlm.gradual_run --data data/gradual-new --config configs/gradual-graph.json --init runs/binding-overfit-sanity-v1/final.mlm --out runs/gradual-curriculum-new --strategy curriculum --stage-steps 500 --stories data/hf/stories/test.jsonl
uv run python -m mlm.gradual_run --data data/gradual-new --config configs/gradual-graph.json --init runs/binding-overfit-sanity-v1/final.mlm --out runs/gradual-flat-new --strategy flat --stage-steps 500 --stories data/hf/stories/test.jsonl
uv run python -m mlm.gradual_eval runs/gradual-curriculum-new/best.mlm --questions data/gradual-new/test-questions.json --out results/gradual-curriculum-new.json
```

Lock both development-selected checkpoints before the last command. Neural candidate ranking uses only textual prompts and learned parameters. Labels and factual metadata only construct/grade the offline dataset; no symbolic answer lookup or regex solver participates in inference. The evaluator preserves raw greedy samples from the first complete group of each bucket, with whitespace/case normalization and no extraction or repair. Those samples are not a full-test generation benchmark.

## Training progression

| Additional updates | Curriculum groups | Complete active training groups | Original group retained | Familiar-name dev groups | New-name dev groups |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | 1 | 1/1 | 100% | 0.0% | 0.0% |
| 500 | 2 | 2/2 | 100% | 0.0% | 2.1% |
| 1000 | 4 | 4/4 | 100% | 6.2% | 16.7% |
| 1500 | 8 | 8/8 | 100% | 2.1% | 16.7% |
| 2000 | 16 | 16/16 | 100% | 0.0% | 20.8% |
| 2500 | 32 | 29/32 | 100% | 0.0% | 41.7% |
| 3000 | 64 | 50/64 | 100% | 2.1% | 29.2% |

The source fits one group; the curriculum preserves that group and fits 2, 4, 8 and 16 groups completely at the recorded endpoints. It drops to 29/32, then 50/64 as new pairings and color assignments are introduced. This is a measured training failure point under this schedule, not proof of a fixed model capacity limit. The flat control fits all 64 training groups by update 2,000 and again at 3,000. Early flat training forgets the seed group, then recovers it.

Both runs finish the full 3,000-update budget. Development selection chooses curriculum step 2,500 (32-group stage) and flat step 2,000 (64 groups). **The reported curriculum test checkpoint therefore predates its final 64-group stage.** The selected curriculum has sampled all eight names and all 20 allowed training entity pairs, but not all 64 eventual color/order groups. Both runs are offered the same budget; their selected update counts and exposure distributions differ as specified by the protocol.

Each arm consumes exactly 1,164,000 input payload bytes and 60,000 supervised payload bytes during the new run. Source, architecture, parameter count (366,722), optimizer settings and budget match; sampling schedules deliberately differ. Adam state continues across stages. The baseline initial source predictions match across both arms. Data/config/source hashes and selection eligibility were verified, then both selected hashes locked before fresh test scoring. Timing is uncontrolled and not a speed benchmark.

## Fresh test results

Two-choice neural likelihood ranking is the primary scoring method. A four-question group requires both color assignments and both queried people for one sentence order. A stricter secondary case requires all eight conditions including both sentence orders. The secondary metric was added after initial development observations, before test scoring; it did not change checkpoint selection. This avoids counting one-order correctness alone as fully order-robust binding.

| Checkpoint | Pool | Individual correct /192 | Complete four-question groups /48 | Complete eight-condition cases /24 |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Source memorization checkpoint | Familiar names, new pairs | 95 | 0 | 0 |
| Source memorization checkpoint | New names | 95 | 0 | 0 |
| Curriculum selected | Familiar names, new pairs | 186 | 42 | 18 |
| Curriculum selected | New names | 122 | 10 | 1 |
| Flat selected | Familiar names, new pairs | 145 | 23 | 11 |
| Flat selected | New names | 150 | 21 | 9 |

Thus the curriculum reaches 96.88% individual accuracy and 18/24 complete order-robust familiar-name cases, but only 63.54% individual and 1/24 robust new-name cases. Flat reaches 75.52% and 11/24 for familiar names, versus 78.13% and 9/24 for new names. The original source has zero robust cases in both pools. There is partial transfer on this controlled task, not just recall of exact training questions, but it is far from reliable name-independent retrieval.

Overall primary four-question test-group correctness is 52/96 curriculum versus 44/96 flat. Overall secondary eight-condition correctness is 19/48 versus 20/48. These measures emphasize different error patterns: there is no clean overall winner. Independent fair random answers have reference probabilities 1/16 for four conditions and 1/256 for eight, but model predictions and examples are dependent; these are not statistical null tests or proof of broad semantic understanding.

Raw greedy samples are fixed before output inspection: the first complete group from each pool (eight total per checkpoint). They score 5/8 for source, 7/8 curriculum and 6/8 flat. This small sample is saved unedited and is not a full-test generation score. Normalization only strips whitespace and case-folds; there is no answer extraction or repair.

## Important split limitation discovered in the audit

A post-hoc construction audit found an avoidable imbalance in the familiar-name split. The initial four training pairs partition people into early pair roles: Dan/Ada/Cal/Fay versus Ned/Ben/Eli/Gus. All four familiar-name development pairs join people from the same early role; all four familiar-name test pairs join opposite early roles. Pair identities are disjoint and texts do not leak, but the two pools are structurally different.

This is particularly relevant because curriculum familiar-name development accuracy is near chance while familiar-name test accuracy is very high. A coarse person-role shortcut could benefit from this structure. The audit does not establish what representation the network actually learned, but it prevents presenting the 18/24 test result as clean evidence of a general entity-matching rule or a robust curriculum advantage. The split I constructed needs a balanced replication across role types and multiple name assignments. Existing results remain preserved rather than silently replacing the test after seeing outcomes.

## English retention and limits

The reused English story monitor starts at loss 4.743716 for the memorization source, already worse than the preserved English checkpoint's 1.121557. Selected curriculum loss is 12.834514 and selected flat loss 10.170839; final endpoints are 13.096501 and 11.697480. This task-only training severely degrades English prediction. Neither model replaces an English/chat checkpoint. No story data enters the new training objective or the selection score.

The current comparison controls architecture, source, learning rate and total offered updates; it does not establish that all curricula are better or worse. Under this schedule, the curriculum gets only 500 updates with all 64 groups available, versus 3,000 in flat training. Longer consolidation or mastery-based progression might change results, but neither was tested. Compared with prior experiments, learning rate, source, name pool and task size changed, so improvements cannot be attributed to one of those factors alone. This is one seed, eight training names, four colors and one shared grammar. It does not establish reliable English chat, broad comprehension, dynamic topology, online inference-time learning or Transformer superiority.

## Decision and verification

Keep the models as research artifacts. The unchanged graph can learn multiple binding cases and transfer partially, but name/pair robustness, benchmark balance and English retention remain unresolved. Before further architecture work, build a fresh role-balanced confirmation split with more varied names and evaluate both known-name new pairings and new-name transfer. Preserve independent development/test pools and monitor English with an explicit retention strategy. Do not retune using this test.

All 47 tests pass, including nested data/split/source checks, persistent optimizer steps, selection eligibility, output protection, and eight-condition grading that rejects one-order luck. Ruff lint/format and source type checks pass. Inference remains entirely neural; labels, pair-role auditing and grouping are offline analysis. No response rules, growing nodes or architecture changes were added in this experiment.

# Gradual binding curriculum

Approved: scale from the already memorized four-question group through more groups, measure novel pairings of familiar names separately from new-name transfer, leave architecture unchanged and monitor English.

Use the sum-readout graph, source runs/binding-overfit-sanity-v1/final.mlm, fresh optimizer at LR 0.003 (the successful sanity LR), batch four, unroll 128, seed 42. The source already has 500 updates of single-group memorization; report that separately. Preserve all sources.

Data: training-name pool Dan/Ned/Ada/Ben/Cal/Eli/Fay/Gus. Reserve four unordered pairs for known-name development and four different pairs for known-name test, each covering all eight names. Remaining 20 pairs supply a deterministic nested 64-group training pool. First group exactly reproduces the source's Dan/Ned gold/blue sanity example; first four groups introduce all eight names, next four reverse their fact order. Add color diversity, then additional name pairings. All four assignment/query swaps remain in each batch. No rehearsal or architecture change. New-name development and test use separate eight-name pools and four disjoint entity pairs per pool. Every evaluation pair includes all six color pairs and both fact orders: 48 complete groups / 192 questions per bucket. Exact texts and held-out pair identities cannot overlap training.

Two arms, identical source and total budget. Curriculum: 500 updates each at 2,4,8,16,32,64 groups, carrying the same optimizer continuously. Flat: 3,000 updates over all 64 groups from the start. Reset recurrent state for independent examples, shuffle complete groups. Evaluate initial state and every 500 updates. Record actual names seen; early familiar-name-pool scores must disclose names not yet trained for binding.

Select among stage endpoints at updates 1,000–3,000 after all eight training names have actually been seen, maximizing macro-average development complete-group accuracy across the two fixed equal-sized buckets, then minimizing combined target loss; exact ties keep earlier state. Initial/500-step metrics are diagnostics, not selection candidates. This avoids selecting before all names have been introduced. Flat uses the same endpoint eligibility. Training scores and English retention do not select checkpoints. Save latest and selected best, stage groups/steps, source/data hashes and RNG/order/cursor. This standalone runner has no resume feature; refuse nonempty outputs.

Tests: nested group counts and first group source-text match, diverse partner coverage, zero exact-text overlap, known-pair partition disjointness, new-name partitioning, balanced four-question groups/masks and unroll limits. End-to-end smoke with small stage budget verifies persistent steps, coverage, selection eligibility, counts and output/source protection. Freeze protocol, config, sources and dataset hashes before training. Lock both selected hashes before opening fresh test questions. Save raw greedy samples, all likelihood scores, per-stage train/known/new-name development results and story retention. One seed, one grammar and a post-hoc source do not establish broad comprehension or a robust causal curriculum benefit.

Implement gradual_data.py and gradual_run.py reusing existing neural/scoring/grouping code. No new inference parser, answer solver, connections, node growth or readout. Update research/PRD/report with actual outcomes, including failures. No repository commit: workspace has no git repository.
